Keep visible kickoff fields in place when tapped, including oversized briefs during keyboard resize.

Terminal's new-chat screen now draws through shared new-chat pieces (layout, mode pill) that the web will reuse. Nothing changes on screen; the Chat | Orchestrator pill's test IDs are now `new-chat-mode*`.

Give Codex workers final-only native subagent reporting, longer waits, and bounded ordinary delegation with reserved QA capacity. Seed bridged Codex-home defaults only where the user has not set a value, preserving user choices and workspace trust.

The shared Audit, Quicklinks and Automations all-activity tables draw their rows as cards below the md breakpoint, so they never scroll sideways on a phone. Terminal's window is wider than that, so its tables are unchanged.

Fix native foreground `focus` and click on the installed host: the adapter compared the host's echoed target with the request's by key order, so every real foreground lease was refused as `lease_mismatch`. It now compares by value, and releases a lease the host admitted but the adapter refused so a reset can settle.

With the unified shell on, a link into another organization's My Work, Servers, Media, Evals, Apps, Settings or Automations page (a notification, a `codepress://open` link, a link in a chat, or a link a page builds) now opens in the embedded web view, where the web picks the organization from the link, instead of being drawn by Terminal under the organization it is on with the other organization's ids. Terminal does not switch organization for it, and the page you were on stays as you left it. A link to an organization you are not in no longer draws anything natively either. Links for the organization Terminal is on, and the window with the unified shell off, are unchanged.

New chat in Chat mode now shows the shared new-chat screen: the coloured "Hello, {name}!" greeting, four starter cards under the input, and Runs on in the row above the input (also in Orchestrator mode).
A project handed off from this Mac now opens as its synced copy when this Mac's cards arrive on the card stream, instead of the read-only tombstone.

The shared shell's phone layout gains a long press on a feed row that opens the row's menu as a bottom sheet, 44 px section-jump buttons, and a search button in the drawer when the host provides one (Terminal's own phone mode is unchanged).
Preserve checkpoint ownership when a retired cloud coding session resumes on a local runner.

Retire graduated Orchestrator rollout settings. Live replies, newest-first chats, pushed project cards, snapshot workers, stacked rail cards, weekly subscription usage, and the document workspace are always available; old stored opt-outs are ignored.
Document why Terminal and Factory operational environment switches are process-wide controls for the feature flag review; behavior and defaults are unchanged.
Prepare the desktop app to run from dependency layers kept outside the app bundle. Nothing changes until a release ships with layers.
Build each macOS architecture in its own release job so arm64 updates and the CLI publish without waiting for the Intel build.

Attribute verified native and proxy Claude requests to retained subscription
windows, with quota/reset history, bounded local HTTP/MCP reports and optional
provenance-preserving usage sync.
Show measured Claude subscription usage by retained five-hour and weekly window in Settings, with quota observations, separate source subtotals and explicit partial coverage.
Reduce server CI disk writes while assembling Terminal's PM SDK runtime, keeping release package copies independent.

Fix the Terminal unit test setup that made MilkdownEditor.test.tsx fail on the Blacksmith runners when the cached Vitest modules were restored: Vitest could not load a stylesheet from the pnpm store outside the checkout. No change to the app.
Restore Cloud VM handoff destinations for accounts in many organizations by scoping project reads to their organization and retaining account-bound Cloud discovery results after the picker deadline.

Let a page that draws its own phone header take the shell's header row and menu button, and let the Orchestrator screen use the shell's drawer instead of its own rail on a phone. Terminal's own layout is unchanged.
Add owner-authenticated live viewing and input transport for the visible browser handoff, with single-use tickets and a shared validated protocol.
Move the kickoff Chat | Orchestrator pill into the unified desktop shell's title bar, centred over the page column.

Settings tabs now tell a group heading, a setting's label and its description apart: headings are larger and bolder, descriptions smaller and muted, and a rule with more room separates one group from the next.
Keep Terminal's shared UI dependency manifest aligned with phone header slots and the shared slide-over primitives.
Draw Hand off… and Project settings as direct buttons in the phone Orchestrator thread's toolbar instead of behind a ⋯ menu.
Website and widget App cards on the Apps page now show their preview instead of a blank face: the window's content security policy lets them frame the App artifact gateway.

Terminal accepts an owner kickoff relayed by the backend (`owner_kickoff`) and starts the project in its owner's own Orchestrator, advertising `orchestrator_owner_kickoff` once Orchestrator messaging is ready.

On a shared computer, a teammate's New Tab, New Workflow and agent launches now open in their own session (created on first use) instead of failing, and the New Workflow dialog names their own subscription or CodePress's relay.

Teammates' Orchestrators and runs now start on a headless `codepress-terminal serve` host, which sets its app version itself. When one cannot start, the teammate sees one sentence naming the computer's owner, the computer and the fix, instead of the raw runtime error.
Servers, My Work and Media stay open while you are on another screen: coming back shows their rows at once and refreshes them in the background, and a hidden Servers page no longer polls.
Cloud mode now opens in a shared-computer window with your own CodePress sign-in, which stays on your machine and never reaches the shared computer.

Settings now looks like Slack's Preferences: a header with a close button, a grouped icon rail on the left and a titled pane on the right, and on a phone a full-screen list of sections that opens one at a time. Four sections are renamed: Terminal app, Agent MCPs, My computers and Local usage.

In a teammate's window on a shared computer, the Files panel now says the computer's files belong to its owner instead of failing to detect a project root, owner-only settings and entry points are hidden, and anything still refused says what it is and who can help instead of "Not available to teammates on this computer".
With the unified shell on, the top of the rail is now the current organization's tile (its logo, avatar or initials) and opens an organization switcher. The foot is the account menu.
The Automations list panel and the Automations page now share one summary read and poll, so Terminal's Automations tab no longer issues a duplicate `/summary` request while the page is open.
Open a waiting browser from its ask on your phone or another Mac, with live touch, keyboard and Paste controls. Browser WebSockets authenticate with a single-use owner ticket.

Shared computers: a teammate's window footer counts their own agents instead of reading "Agents unavailable". The computer owner's tabs, which an admin teammate can see, are badged as the owner's, dimmed and read-only, and the owner's output, input and attention text (such as their account errors) are kept from the teammate. The owner's settings gear is hidden in a teammate's window, and the session and worktree refusals name the owner when they are signed in.

With the Unified shell on, Settings opens as the same Slack-style modal as the dialog, grouped Account, Organization and This machine, over whatever section you were on, instead of a page in the list panel. Pages that live on the web, such as Billing, are marked with an external-link icon and close the modal to open in the web layer. Escape or the close button returns you to where you were.
Refuse retired live browser viewer actions after another daemon replaces the shared-profile handoff.

Repository kickoff now follows each person's own "Repository kickoff" switch in the web app's Feature Flags menu instead of an organization setting. It is off until you turn it on, and Terminal picks the change up within a minute: with it on, a new chat or Orchestrator project offers repositories instead of a Project folder.
The Chat | Orchestrator pill now slides its white thumb to the option you pick, with a short spring and a pop on the label, instead of swapping instantly.
Return live browser links from machine handoffs and guide agents to share them for human-only browser steps.
Add a Build panel setting under Settings → Orchestrator → Display (Last used, Open or Closed) that chooses whether a project's Work and Plan panel starts open in a wide window.

New workflows and new sessions now open their first tab in Ghostty when Ghostty is turned on, instead of always falling back to xterm. Every new terminal tab now goes through one shared admission step.
My Work, Media, Servers and Evals show the rows you last saw as soon as you open them, even after relaunching, then quietly update them from the server. Signing out deletes what was stored.
Pressing Design, Integrations or an App page now shows the page only once its content is on screen, and a page that reloads on its own no longer makes the next press wait out the timeout.

The unified shell's rail popups (organization switcher, account menu, machine picker, More) draw the theme's border colour instead of a white or black outline, with 12px corners, a shadow and small muted section labels, and open just past the rail. The current organization is marked by its check alone. Kit menus, selects, dialogs and sheets in Terminal also stop drawing their border in the text colour.
Publish a project's snapshot to its cloud copy as soon as it arrives on a Mac by direct move or takeover, so a later takeover never starts from the old home's copy.
Moving a project back onto a Mac that handed it off now goes through when the cloud still holds that Mac's own copy, continuing here at a generation the next direct move cannot collide with.
Settings → General now has a "Sessions and remote access" section with "Keep cloud copies of sessions" and "Remote agent actions". Organization admins can turn either off; members see them read-only.
Use the shared phone shell header for Orchestrator projects, with compact progress, the hosting machine and Work actions.
Show one "Picked up" line after a takeover, and share a running takeover between presses of the same project.
Ship seeded installers, a slim updater archive and separately signed dependency layers with every release, so a later update can download only what changed.

Apps and Automations show the rows you last saw as soon as you open them, even after relaunching, then quietly update them from the server. Each part of the page loads on its own, so it fills in as soon as its own answer arrives.

Settings calls the per-computer group "Computer · <name>" instead of "This machine", and the autocompact token contract and model catalog now come from the shared UI package so the web's Account → Agents page edits the same value with the same rules.

Subscription failover, PR readiness approval, review delivery, working hours, appearance and the agent automation toggles now follow your account across computers. Each Mac hands its own choices to your account once, the first time the account has none, and keeps them as its fallback; a change on one Mac reaches the others at their next refresh. New local Orchestrator projects start from your account's merge and prompt-approval defaults.
Update by downloading the slim app and only the dependency layers that changed, falling back to the full bundle on any failure.
A project that moved away from this Mac names where it went and can move again here or to a Cloud VM, including when that Mac is away and no cloud copy exists to continue from.
Mark retained MicroVM modules as deprecated so future agent work uses the ECS runner hosts.
Offer Hand off… on a project this Mac recorded as moved when sync is on, and add Continue here to the Moved banner.
Integrations is no longer its own rail entry: it is a row of Settings, and choosing it shows the web page beside the Settings list as Billing does.

After launch, My Work, Servers, Media, Evals, Apps and Automations quietly read their first page in the background, all at once, so the first press of each shows its rows with no loading skeleton. Nothing is read with Save-Data on, and a refresh that returns what is already shown no longer redraws the rows.

A chat or Orchestrator project started with repositories now opens worktrees off origin's default branch of Terminal's own managed clone (cloned the first time), never of a checkout of yours. A chat with repositories and no Project folder starts in the first repository's worktree. The remote kickoff's repository refusal now says the switch is yours.
Bundle the shared shell's pending-section state for phone drawer taps. Terminal draws no phone shell, so nothing changes on screen.

A stored page that no longer matches what the app expects can no longer break a section. Saved rows from a different app version are ignored and cleared, and a section that fails to draw saved rows clears them and loads again once.
The live terminal viewer for another machine's Orchestrator panes now runs on a shared stream client that can open any live terminal stream. Pane terminals look and behave as before.

Terminal can now stream any of its terminal tabs live, and open a new shell in a "Remote" session, for you on codepress.dev and the phone app. The web side ships in a later release. A new switch, Settings → Network → "Allow terminal from web & phone" (on by default), turns all of it off for this computer. The switch is also available as `allowRemoteTerminal` in `update_terminal_agent_settings`.

With the unified shell on, the Settings modal draws every section in its own pane, the web pages included (Integrations, Platform MCP, Team computers, Branding, Billing, Capacity, App hosting, Usage). Choosing one, or following a link to one, keeps the modal open; Escape, ⌘W and the close button return you to where you were.

Automations no longer reads the whole automation list again every time its activity summary refreshes. A running workflow's agent log now loads only its newest messages, and its step list leaves out the step inputs and outputs it never shows.

Settings → Account in Terminal draws the same Orchestrator, Agent accounts, Agents, Notifications and My computers pages as the web and the phone, in the shell's Settings modal and in the Settings dialog. The Computer tabs keep only what belongs to this computer: model defaults, the agent feed, the cloud copy, the step check, working hours, feature flags, compaction windows, the automation and pull-request switches, failover, keep-updated and each repository rule's merge choice now live on the Account page, and each leaves one line that opens it. The Computer group is named "Computer · <this computer>".
Add an extra Pinned section and Pin / Unpin actions for One-feed projects and chats, with cloud pins across computers and local offline mirrors.

A live terminal viewer on the web or the phone can fit the tab to its own window. It joins the tab's size like another window: the narrowest one wins, so while the Mac's window shows the tab it can only shrink it, and the tab gets its size back when the viewer lets go or leaves.
Folding the unified shell's list with ⌘\ now eases it shut and open over 200ms instead of snapping, and dragging the sidebar's resize handle follows the cursor without lagging behind it.

The Orchestrator's chat rail and Details panel now slide in and out over 200ms on desktop instead of snapping. The drawer terminal resizes once, at the final width, rather than on every frame of the slide.
Open a task handed off to the cloud in the Agent tab from its retained card.
Restore the Mac CLI publish, which refused every delivery because the ledger records a release ID only after the macOS lane completes.
Carry attachments and conversation mentions into projects started on your computer from the web or phone.
Hand a Terminal tab off to the agent runner from any organization: the Cloud destination no longer needs Coding VM Workspaces, and a task brought back into its tab keeps syncing.
A Cloud handoff the backend refuses now shows the backend's reason, such as the organization's concurrent session limit, instead of only a status code.
Let the Mac arm64 and Intel release builds run at the same time on one machine.
Linux releases build faster by restoring the Rust cache and skipping work on unchanged layers.
A Claude task brought back from Cloud into its tab keeps syncing to its cloud chat.
Track the shared phone viewport helper in Terminal's UI dependency closure.
Share Terminal's motion tokens and existing keyframes with codepress.dev while preserving Terminal's curves and timing.

Carry attachments and conversation mentions when starting projects on shared computers. Older computers receive signed file links and conversation references in the brief without blocking Send or showing a carry notice.
Make Work push the complete unified phone shell left with the shared phone panel animation, including the header and tabs.
Track the shared shell search field in Terminal's UI dependency closure so shared shell changes receive browser verification. Terminal's own search bar remains a separate change.

The one agent feed, the unified shell and Orchestrator prompt customization are on for everyone: Terminal no longer reads the retired feed, shell, sync and instructions flags, and Settings → Orchestrator drops the Agent feed switches. Cards always sync; transcripts, snapshots, checkpoints and machine load follow only the admin's copies setting, and a copy endpoint that answers 404 is read quietly as copies off.
New Mac installs download their dependencies on first launch, with progress on the setup screen and automatic retries.
Add global search to the desktop title bar with Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+L, sharing the web palette UI. Move the Chat | Orchestrator switch back into the Agent new-chat page.
Keep the cloud project import in step with what Terminal exports.
Track the shared project placeholder helper in Terminal's UI dependency closure so shared UI changes select Terminal verification.

The title-bar search is now a small "Search ⌘⇧L" pill beside the update button, so it no longer covers the Agent project toolbar. It also finds project files: with an Agent project open, matching files appear under Files and open in the Files view. The separate file-search icon beside the Thread and Files tabs is gone; Cmd/Ctrl+P still opens file search.
Show the selected project's known title, status and machine while its thread loads, without displaying another project's thread.

Round edge-to-edge phone drawer cards and extend both drawers and shell lists to the screen bottom while keeping controls clear of the home indicator. Animate their slide using translation and opacity with static edge and shadow paint.

Orchestrator: with the Agent feed on, New on the All kind opens the kickoff in the mode of the conversation on screen, Orchestrator for an open project and Chat for an open chat, instead of the last pill pick.
A headless Terminal home now answers a synced copy's project actions, so Dismiss on a question works from your phone or another machine instead of failing with "didn't answer".

A project's tab row is complete from the moment it opens: Plans is there in every phase and says "No plan yet" until there is one, and a project on another Mac shows Files and Terminal straight away, each saying why while the Mac is offline or still connecting.

Terminal macOS releases no longer get stuck on the build machine when clearing the previous build's leftovers is briefly refused. The clean-up now retries, and finishes a half-done clean-up itself on the next release.
Share Terminal's Auto device mapping with web and phone while preserving Terminal's existing router behavior.

Apps keeps each card's loaded preview when you come back to it in the same session, instead of blanking every card and reloading every preview. A kept preview link is never reused once it has expired.
Keep new-chat controls in one row and support host options in the shared + menu, with one model and effort chip.
Default Terminal Chat kickoff to Auto, using the existing owned-machine routing and This machine fallback.
Terminal releases reach users faster: admission and publishing take less time, CLI packaging no longer holds up the desktop build, and each delivery reports how long every lane took.

Give the background daemon 30 seconds instead of 10 to start when Terminal launches, so a slow first launch (an Intel Mac opening a just-installed update) no longer closes the app. `CODEPRESS_DAEMON_START_TIMEOUT_MS` overrides the wait.
Show organization icons through authenticated cached thumbnails in the switcher and General settings. Load visible rows on demand and reuse images when the switcher reopens.
Launch Terminal-local Kimi Orchestrators through a renewable loopback relay with explicit account choice and provider-aware recovery.
Linux builds and CLIs now ship alongside Mac instead of after it, and CLI publishing is faster.

The Orchestrator rail and feed share one selected colour, the phone rail marks the active item with a slim pill, count pills are slimmer, tabs and cards share one left edge, and the Search field fills the feed's top row.
Keep list_machines available when control discovery fails, and recover missing controls on partial discovery pages.
Always cover all CodePress organizations in personal Terminal MCP connections and show coverage read-only in Settings.
Show kickoff sending progress in the send button instead of a separate starting-project row.
Let the owner browse recent folders and directories on this computer from the web app through the read-only device folder protocol.
Keep synced project composers quiet while loading, then enable replies normally. Name the home machine when a Local only project cannot accept replies.
Publish Linux CLI updates sooner after a release, with the same contents, signing and verification.
Let local Orchestrators post HTML from a file path and reuse mockups without repeating their markup in the transcript.

The Orchestrator now plans an edge-case inventory for every change and a layout matrix for UI work, and views each screen's screenshots itself before reporting a UI pull request, building the layout matrix from the diff when the plan has none or misses a screen.
Upload synced Orchestrator HTML posts to CodePress and include render pointers in synced thread reads.
Hand a local Orchestrator project off to the cloud agent runner from the Hand off dialog and MCP tools.

Terminal's read-only git calls (status, repository discovery, the editor gutter, checkout inspection, project session worktree reads, handoff dirty checks, the dirty check before a worktree is removed, managed preview checkouts) no longer take git's optional `.git/index.lock`, so a read killed by its timeout can no longer leave a stale lock that blocks commits.
Orchestrator thread posts with an HTML render show their page again instead of an "origin is not allowed" error.
Warm the phone drawer and its list after idle so opening avoids mounting them during the slide, while preserving closed-state accessibility, focus and native reporting.
Show the unified shell in signed-in computer windows and open web-only pages in the browser when the window has no web pane.

Use the shared feed open target decision across Terminal and web, preserving
Terminal card lookup and handoff behavior. Recognize org-root cloud chat links
and handle malformed chat URLs with the shared web parser.
Show synced project HTML posts from CodePress storage, including while the home computer sleeps, with text fallback while loading.
Test tooling only: Terminal's title-bar layout test uses the shared `@codepress/e2e-layout` collision helper, and its e2e selector selects the specs that import it. No change to the app.
Offer Hand off on a project this Mac moved to the cloud, so its Orchestrator can come back here, and deliver messages sent to its old address to the cloud project.

Terminal keeps each tab folder's branch and origin answer warm when another repository's refs change, follows `[include]` and `includeIf "gitdir:"` config files instead of re-running Git, and stops re-reading folders that are not repositories, so the server spawns far fewer `git branch` / `git remote get-url` processes.

Orchestrators start sooner: the instructions refresh, MCP status, runtime preparation, Platform MCP preparation and the account env now run while the project's session worktree is prepared, a new session worktree is made with one fetch of origin instead of four, and each start logs a `pm start timing` line.
Use saved personal Orchestrator and Workers models for kickoffs without explicit model picks.

The unified shell's machine picker now lists your Remote Access computers, and each online one opens from its own row: a terminal icon connects it in this window and the window icon opens it in a new window. The "Open another computer…" row is gone.

Use the shared repository and optional folder chips for Chat and Project kickoff. Start with up to ten repositories on a computer, preserve the single-repository Cloud payload, and offer a compatible folder path with an update message on older Terminals. Retire the repository kickoff toggle.
Open synced projects and chats immediately from the feed, fetching a missing copy by id with a retry for connection failures.

Pressing Send on a local Orchestrator kickoff opens the project thread right away, showing "Starting the Orchestrator…" while the PM launches in the background. A launch that fails still leaves the project open with the Orchestrator recovery ask. Your agent defaults are cached for a minute so the kickoff no longer waits on that read.

Terminal now reads the Ghostty engine's build record from the installed app at runtime instead of baking it into the frontend, so Apple Silicon and Intel Macs ship the same frontend and macOS releases build it once. Ghostty stays available on Apple Silicon and unavailable on Intel (xterm renders), as before.

New Orchestrator projects start sooner: while the kickoff composer is open, Terminal prepares a spare worktree of the Project folder's repository, and the project's start claims it instead of running `git worktree add`. Unused spares are removed after 30 minutes, on Terminal start and by storage cleanup.

Hosted macOS Terminal releases now install one frontend built on Linux instead of building it on each slow Mac runner, after checking it was built from the same commit, version and Node. If that build is missing or does not match, the Mac builds the frontend itself as before.
Let computer chats use connected repositories through managed per-chat worktrees, with an optional git folder and safe worktree cleanup.
The icon rail has a Search button under the org logo that opens global search (⌘⇧L); the title-bar search pill stays.
Time the first project opened after launch as one `[Renderer:Open]` log line, reported as `open` in `get_terminal_diagnostics`.

Kimi Orchestrators keep working through brief CodePress outages and token rotation. A slow or failed account or settings check no longer ends a turn with "401 The selected Kimi account is unavailable": the held token stays in use until it expires, renewals happen ahead of rotation and expiry, and the relay answers 503 ("CodePress unreachable; retrying") for a temporary gap or 401 with the specific reason when access is really withdrawn.

Headless Terminal: cross-machine tools now wait (up to 15 s, `CODEPRESS_MACHINE_CHANNEL_WAIT_MS`) for a device-channel reconnect instead of failing at once, retry read-only machine operations once after a reconnect, and name the real refusal code instead of asking you to sign in. Terminal's own Computer Use entry from an earlier headless-CLI install is now refreshed to the current install.

Clicking a rail row right after a restart draws the project's header (name, machine, phase) and its loading rows at once, and this Mac's projects show their posts as soon as the daemon answers their snapshot, without waiting for the project list or the organization list.
Handoff progress dialog: the current-step dot now pulses and is no longer clipped, and the footer divider is gone.

Kimi accounts can now be saved On this machine: Settings → Agents → Add account → Kimi → On this machine signs in with Kimi's device code. The account is stored in Terminal's encrypted pool, refreshed locally, and can be paused, removed or chosen as this computer's Kimi account. A chosen Local account serves Kimi Orchestrators directly, with no CodePress lease.

Browser handoffs now get a live view when a Chrome window from an earlier Terminal run is still open on the profile: an owned start closes it safely (sign-ins kept) and opens a fresh one, and an owner's complete can close it. On Linux hosts with no display the handoff browser runs as a full Chrome on a private Xvfb display (headless only when Xvfb is missing, with a note that bot checks may refuse it) and is reached through live view, and a handoff browser that dies at launch is reported as an error instead of a silent success. Completing a handoff now closes its Chrome gracefully, so a sign-in made just before complete is kept.
Terminal logs the code and reason each time its device channel closes, so a dropped connection can be explained afterwards.

Keep the Orchestrator and Workers chips when a settings read fails or you switch projects: failed reads retry by themselves, a synced copy re-reads when it comes back live, and each project's last settings show at once on return.
Settings reads the organization's new Local-first routing flag, ready for the routing sections that follow.

`@` opens the same menu in every Orchestrator composer mode, and answers and blocker replies carry the picks to the Orchestrator as a message does. A pick that can't be delivered is refused at send with the draft kept.
A notification alone no longer cancels an account switch, and a switch that has landed is never reported as failed. Every stopped switch now says why in the log.

Kimi usage left now shows wherever it does for Claude and Codex. A Local Kimi account's card shows its 5-hour and weekly bars with reset times and Refresh usage, and a selected Kimi model shows the active account's weekly usage in the Orchestrator and worker pickers, whichever scope the account has. Terminal reads Kimi only for Local accounts; Personal and Team usage comes from CodePress. If a usage check fails, the last reading stays and is marked out of date.

Read this Mac's Orchestrator project list once at launch: the list keys its store by the cached organization while access loads, and the first account restore keeps the read in flight instead of starting over.
Phone feed rows: one tap on the time opens the row's menu, its items work on the first tap, and neither an item nor a tap outside the menu closes the side nav.
Terminal windows now paint their chrome outline in your theme before any script runs, and the app renders without waiting on IPC or the network.
Synced copies keep their Orchestrator and Workers chips while the home is away; pressing one says which computer needs to be awake.

Terminal's sidebar now loads sessions, workflows and tabs without waiting for the WebSocket, and a relaunch shows your last-known sessions right away (read-only, marked as connecting) until live data replaces them.

Every online machine, desktop or headless, now reports its CPU, RAM and power for Auto on every heartbeat, with no organization setting in the way. A failed checkout or probe read costs only that field. A machine that stops reporting reads "Not reporting load · last seen 4m ago" (or "· never") in Runs on instead of a plain "Online", one on an outdated Terminal reads "Update Terminal to route here", and `get_terminal_diagnostics` shows `load_reporting`.

Gemini workers now say plainly what Google allows on a personal account: one warning at sign-in, at first pick and in the project thread, linking Google's FAQ and steering to an API key. A dead `agy` login shows Reconnect, and agents can read worker sign-in status.

Secure Access now covers the git, pull request, workflow and agent hook routes, so a tunnel URL alone can no longer merge a pull request or change hooks. A teammate's Diff tab says whose files these are instead of showing a status code.
On a synced copy, `@` now lists the same chats whatever the home runs, and answers and blocker replies carry their picks to the home. A home too old to take them refuses at send with the draft kept.
Remote Browser Tabs refuse malformed preview ports and always sandbox hostile preview responses.

Sign-in on a tunnel now only returns to a path on the same machine, so a crafted `/auth` link can no longer run script or send you to another site. Deep links keep their path, query and hash through sign-in.
Remote access: a page on another `*.codepress.dev` host can no longer use a visitor's tunnel cookie to read files or open previews.

Measure every step of a cold launch: the app's own marks since its process started, the window's page, script, first commit, first paint, chrome and session marks, and the kind of launch (first run, relaunch, attach, after an update), shown in Terminal diagnostics. An update restart's stages now reach the new process's diagnostics.
Keep one checked record of what each subscription provider supports, so new provider work starts from what the code does today. Nothing changes in Terminal.

`kimi` in a Terminal tab now runs on this computer's chosen Kimi account (Local, Personal or Team) without `kimi login`, whether typed in a shell tab or started with the tab. Each tab gets a private Kimi Code home that reaches Kimi through Terminal's loopback relay on a local token revoked when the tab closes, and conversation history stays shared with your own `~/.kimi-code`. With no account chosen, `kimi` runs as it always did. Kimi Orchestrators share the same relay.

A new install opens the real Terminal window as soon as the server runtime is downloaded, instead of after every runtime layer. The agent runtime and the computer-use Driver keep downloading in parallel behind it, with an install banner that shows progress, a failed attempt and a Retry button. Terminals work right away, and local agents and computer use report that they are still installing and start once their layer lands, without a restart.
An account switch now tells you what happened: switched, still switching, replaced by a newer choice, or failed with the real reason. Accounts and the agent tools use the same words.

The Orchestrator rail's remembered rows draw on a relaunch again, even though the auth broker renumbers the credential at launch, and each organization's preferences are read once per launch instead of twice. The launch line now also says when the feed's headers came back, when access answered, and how long the main thread stalled before the first rows.

On a synced copy, `@` now lists files from the home's Project folder, and a picked file reaches the home's Orchestrator from a message, an answer or a blocker reply. A home too old to take them refuses at send with the draft kept. When a file search can't answer, the menu says so instead of showing nothing.

Quick tunnels: owner access now uses a real secret that signing out of the desktop revokes, and only the desktop's own account can claim the machine. Quick-tunnel owners sign in once more after updating.

Remote Browser Tab previews are now bound to the port they were opened for. Each port has its own preview cookie, and apps can no longer widen a Service Worker over other ports. Apps that call a sibling dev port from a remote preview are refused unless that port is also open in the same browser.

Restarting into an update is faster. Every window's server is stopped at once, the relaunch follows the old app's exit more closely, and copying the background server's new version no longer delays the first window. With the background service, a new server that is still restoring your sessions no longer takes over from the old one. Each stage of the restart is now timed in Terminal diagnostics (`update_restart`).
Add the shared feed notice to the Agent list's component, for Terminal to adopt next. Terminal's feed looks the same until it does.
Machine picker: a headless CLI service machine now shows the terminal and new-window icons instead of Open CodePress, and `list_machines` no longer says CodePress is closed on it.
Draw the desktop window right away, in the person's theme, while the PTY broker and daemon start behind it, and stop repeating login-shell Node discovery and the server bundle hash on every launch.

Terminal relaunch connects the window while saved tabs restore: tabs are created in slices with the window's last tab first, and requests for a tab that is still restoring wait for it instead of failing.
Forwarded traffic is never local: a loopback request with forwarding headers needs a credential, and while Tailscale serves, every loopback caller's account is checked.
Keep Settings open when the window crosses the phone width, so a sign-in in progress keeps its device code or pasted code.

Settings → Local checkouts now shows a working "Choose folder…" on remote machines and in the browser, listing the viewed machine's folders; hosts without the browse endpoint keep the typed path input.
Terminal can add a folder to its local checkout allowlist when its owner asks over the device-folders channel.

Terminal updates no longer wait on a slow checkout read before connecting, and PR events no longer run `git remote get-url` for every directory of a repository that uses `extensions.worktreeConfig`, or for tabs in deleted folders.

Gemini workers now notice a Google quota limit: the Orchestrator hears it, a strip offers another provider's model, and the same login resumes at its reset when the time is known. `agy` conversations resume on relaunch, and a Stop hook reports turn ends where `agy` runs hooks. Terminal never switches Google accounts.
Keep the launch report when an update moves the window to a new background server, and restart the feed's startup backoff on the new server.
Chats can run in any folder on this computer, git checkout or not. Add the folder to Local checkouts in Settings; your home folder and Terminal's data folder are still refused.

Add a macOS sandbox for work sent to a machine. Each job runs in its own Linux VM that sees only its repo, with Apple's `container` on macOS 26 and Lima on older Macs. Nothing routes to it yet; machines report whether they can run it.
With Local-first routing on, a wrapped command now waits for the room its own history says it needs, and a command that needs little reserves only what it uses.
Keep a computer you own as an Auto and Move candidate after you share it with teammates.

Grok is refused as a local Orchestrator with a sentence saying why, before any session opens. A project already saved on a Grok Orchestrator keeps its record, thread and worker settings, and its start fails with that sentence. A Grok organization default moves to a signed-in Orchestrator provider.

Repository rules can now block Grok on its own, and a Grok worker is no longer owned by the Codex rule. So a rule with `subscriptions.codex: blocked` stops blocking Grok workers, and a rule with `subscriptions.codex: {kind: "account"}` stops attaching Codex pool flags to one. Set a `grok` entry to block Grok.

Grok model pickers now say a model runs on a Grok subscription or an xAI API key, and Terminal's managed Grok runtime moves to 1.0.70.

Share links are now view-only: they follow the terminal's output, cannot type, and can't reach files, previews or desktop capture. The shared window shows a View only label, and the share settings say what a link allows.

Terminal windows, phones and browsers start faster: the code every window downloads before drawing drops from 10.8 MB to 5.2 MB, and its main script to 4.3 MB. The code editor, Settings, the file explorer, the diff view and other panes not on the first screen now load the first time you open them. If one can't be fetched, for example on an offline phone, the pane says so and offers Retry, and the rest of the app keeps working.
Shared phone header code gains a borderless option and keeps header order by mount. Terminal does not draw this header, so nothing changes on screen.

Capacity hosts size automation jobs from the backend's forecast envelope when it sends one, advertise their own budget so placement stops sending work they would refuse, and report overrun kills so the forecast learns.

The Orchestrator feed appears sooner after a restart or update when the backend is slow: once the cloud's list is in hand, the feed no longer waits for a separate check of whether the cloud is reachable.
Reloading right after switching workflows now comes back to that workflow.

A launch on an account in hundreds of organizations no longer reads every organization at once: the open organization reads first, the rest wait for the first rows and go out a few at a time, and a row that needs an answer still on its way shows as loading, not off.
A project opened from another machine lists its workers' terminals on the Terminal tab again, and its Work rows can open them.
Runs on: a machine that stopped reporting load never shows a percentage, and machine rows keep their load when Auto falls back or an attempt is held.

Hand off… a session the cloud holds to this Mac, from its tab's card, the Agent tab or the handoff tools. Claude resumes in a new tab at the cloud's latest confirmed code; Codex continues in this Mac's Agent tab. A tab whose session moved shows one card that names where it runs now (the cloud, a tab on a Mac, or a Mac's local runtime) with the way to reach it. Bring back here is gone.

A project on another computer now shows any file, not only text. Images, video, audio and PDFs open in the Files view, and every other file gets a card with its size and a Download button. Files over 25 MB wait for Load or Download, and files over 500 MB are refused with their size. Viewing needs the Terminal on the other computer to be updated too; until it is, the file says so.

Settings → Agents → Accounts now shows one provider at a time, in tabs for Claude, Codex, Muse, Kimi, Grok and Google, and Add account lists only the selected provider's options. A tab with something waiting, such as a Reconnect or a sign-in in progress, shows a warning dot. The last tab you viewed reopens.

Remote access now requires sign-in by default. A quick tunnel starts only while you're signed in on this computer and belongs to that account, and turning Secure Access off is an explicit choice with a warning.

A phone or browser on a tunnel whose local projects are refused now gets the owner sign-in on New chat, and stays there when the feed falls back. The mobile app's loader also waits for the launch screen to settle, up to 5 seconds.

Terminal issues a credential to its window, tabs, hooks and helpers, and logs any local call without one. For an organization with local-first routing on, reaching the loopback port is no longer enough: a caller with no credential is refused unless the kernel shows it descends from a live tab, an agent can't change consent or reach another machine without a grant in project settings, and another account's process is demoted on every machine.
Report running placement reservations on each heartbeat, and claim a sandbox only after its canary has passed for this runtime version.

For an organization with local-first routing on, a local Browser Tab now opens through a preview address only Terminal's window can get. A process that reaches Terminal's port can no longer use it to reach other services on this machine. The address changes once when the setting turns on, so an app open in a Browser Tab starts with empty cookies and storage that one time.

Save several Grok accounts in Settings → Agents → Accounts: Add account → On this machine on the Grok tab shows a link and a code you can approve from any device, and you can cancel it or come back to it after a reload. Your `~/.grok` is never read or written. Saved accounts can be paused, removed and reconnected. Nothing runs on a saved account yet.

Agents can no longer widen a machine's exposure over MCP. `update_terminal_agent_settings` refuses turning on remote desktop, terminal from web and phone, Computer Use and other consent settings, or adding folders; `set_network_access` refuses loosening the IP allowlist; and `set_tailscale_enabled` refuses turning the tailnet address on. Each refusal names the Settings screen a person uses instead. Turning these off or tightening them still works, and `update_terminal_agent_settings` now accepts only a local agent or a verified call from your own device.
The unified shell stays on when the agent feed can't be reached. The Agent list says so over its last rows, with Retry, and an organization switch no longer flashes the old layout.
A computer picks up a rotated tunnel token by itself, at launch, at sign-in, or when told over its device channel, and renaming or deleting a tunnel clears the sign-in left on its old address.

Workers can now run on a Kimi model. Choosing Kimi K3.1 Pro as the worker model launches Claude Code on this computer's chosen Kimi account through Terminal's local relay, with its own worktree, hooks and token. With no account chosen, the org toggle off, or this computer not approved, the assignment is refused with that reason. A Kimi worker stays on the account it started on, and Claude account failover never applies to it.

For an organization with local-first routing on, Settings shows "What can run on this Mac". Turning on "Accept workers", "Accept jobs", "Run my automations" or a personal-data grant takes the macOS administrator dialog. Agents can read these and ask for them, but can't set them, and turning one off never needs a password.
A packaged window, popout or file viewer now sends its secret to its own daemon, so it keeps working when local-first routing is turned on.

A teammate using a shared computer can start agents again: New Workflow types its start command in their tab without the owner's Computer Use launch, and `claude` or `codex` falls back to the copy Terminal staged for teammates when they have none of their own.

Measure what each task costs in CPU and RAM, including servers, deploys, workers and Orchestrators, and report it while the organization's Local-first routing flag is on. `pnpm heavy` accepts the `deploy`, `server` and `install` classes.

Video, audio, PDFs, Browser Tab files and plan pages load with a short-lived capability from the window when the org's local-first routing flag is on, so a process that forges browser headers can no longer read a file through the daemon's loopback port.
Keep the Mac sandbox's caches per owner, repo and branch, stop jobs at their disk limit, destroy leftover sandbox VMs on start, and fail fast when a stored registry login does not answer.

Local agent sessions now report when a plain `git checkout` moves them to another branch. With local-first routing on, this release is also the first that can be refused a Factory write on a branch another member owns; the message names the way out, and the Factory CLI reports it as a refusal rather than an unreachable lineage store.
A terminal tab reloaded by "Keep Only Recent Terminals Loaded" no longer shows its history twice.
Letters typed right after picking an @ mention stay in the order you typed them.

Gemini workers can run on a Gemini API key from Settings → Agents → Accounts → Google, with a Local, Personal or Team key. Workers run through a relay on this computer, so the key stays out of their environment, settings and logs, and your own `agy` keeps its login. Usage shows at per-token billing, and repository rules can pin a key.

A chosen key that can't serve refuses the launch rather than falling back to your Google sign-in. If you downgrade to a release without this feature, workers go back to `agy`'s own config, which may be your Google sign-in. Personal and Team keys need the matching CodePress update; Local keys work without it. Windows isn't supported yet.
With local-first routing on, a Mac's Remote Desktop frames reach the daemon over the direct channel again, so desktop use on a locked session keeps working.

Local Kimi account cards show the account's current usage again: Terminal now reads the `usages` windows that Kimi's own client reads, and a window with no use yet reads as 0% instead of leaving the card on its last reading.

Keep native Claude and Codex tabs attached to their running agents after an update or relaunch, and restore a native tab that must start a new shell once its account is ready instead of leaving it without one.

With the organization's Local-first routing flag on, a test run sized from past measurements now gets only the workers memory supports, instead of every core it wants because an earlier smaller run fit.
Kimi Orchestrators and workers no longer send every MCP tool schema on every call, which could reach hundreds of thousands of tokens per call on a machine with many connected tools.

Terminal signs its calls that start or drive work on a machine, so a sign-in copied off this computer can later be told apart from this computer. Settings > Computers shows a computer whose key isn't confirmed yet and how to confirm it. An Orchestrator's reach to your other machines now follows the project its credential was issued for. Nothing is refused for a missing signature yet.
Terminal now holds its port on both `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`, so a `localhost` connection from the window can't reach another process listening on the other address.

For an organization with local-first routing on, the menu bar and Settings offer "Stop all work sent to this Mac". It destroys the sandboxes of work your other machines sent here and refuses anything new, with no password and no backend, and it survives a restart. Turning it off asks for this Mac's password, and stopped jobs don't come back. Agents can read it but can't change it.
Terminal now signs more of the calls that add a machine or decide where work runs, ready for the backend to require proof on them.

A remote owner's sign-in no longer fails when an unrelated setting is saved during it. If the computer still can't confirm the sign-in, the page asks again a few times, then shows a plain message with a way to try again.

Revoking a share link, retiring an owner session or turning on Secure Access now ends connections that are already open. A backend outage never closes one, and an owner who's signed out this way reconnects without a sign-in prompt. Only the desktop can send screen frames and WebRTC offers, and only the owner can restart a machine for an update.

Hand off a session the cloud holds to any of your Macs. Hand off… on a cloud session now lists This Mac first, then your other Macs: online ones you can pick, and asleep, offline or out-of-date ones greyed out with the reason. Picking another Mac asks it to take the session over and shows its steps here until it resumes there. This Mac now also receives sessions handed to it from another Mac or the web.
Settings > Usage on a phone-width window: a bar tapped just as the chart first appears keeps its breakdown instead of being cleared a moment later.
On a Linux host with no screen, the private display behind the live browser view no longer resets when its browser closes, so the next browser can connect to it right away instead of being refused.

Rendered tab output reads the lines that have text again: a tab whose output did not fill its screen, such as a fresh shell or a TUI drawn at the top of a tall window, no longer reads as empty on codepress.dev's Terminal page or in an Orchestrator's worker reads. If a render ever comes back empty for a tab with output, the read answers the raw tail and logs a warning.
Record each subscription provider's terms on limits, and require a `failover` row to cite its terms. No behaviour change.

A headless Terminal reads its organization's Local-first routing flag and uploads usage samples over its device channel. With the flag on it measures its tasks and enforces local-client credentials like a signed-in Mac; off, nothing changes.

Muse accounts now show 5-hour and weekly usage on each card, from the last reading taken while that account was active, "Usage unknown" when there is none, and a Reconnect button when a login stops working.

Signed out, the Agent screen now says what the Orchestrator does and offers sign-in right there, instead of one line of text. While a browser sign-in is in progress, the sign-in options now show which provider is waiting and a Cancel button, instead of an email form.
Show the usage-limit strip on any Claude or Codex agent stopped at its limit, not only rule-bound ones. A limit that automatic account switching is handling still shows nothing.
Orchestrator projects stay usable after a Terminal's own machine id changes, and Open live browser now works on Linux hosts.

A failed first-launch download now says what went wrong and offers Try again and Install Node.js, so it recovers without restarting the app. A runtime download that makes no progress for a while says so and keeps trying. A Node.js download whose connection goes silent now fails with Try again instead of hanging.

Orchestrator: the New chat screen (and feed tabs and the automation pane) now shows Collapse sidebar in the rail toolbar, like an open chat, so the toolbar no longer shifts. Collapsing shows the same slim strip, and the open/closed choice is shared with the thread screen.

Add "What ran here" to a computer's row in Settings, listing what reached that computer and who sent it, when its organization has local-first routing on. Each consent change on this Mac is reported to that list, and a failed report never changes the consent. A heartbeat now names every recent stop of all work, not only the last, so stops made offline all reach that list.

The "Your session expired" sign-in prompt now opens only after a session really expired or was rejected. Someone who never signed in, or who signed out on purpose, no longer sees it on every launch. It stays off Agent's signed-out screen, which already offers sign-in, and a session ending while Agent is open keeps you on Agent instead of switching to Terminal. Dismissing the prompt now lasts across restarts until the next sign-in or expiry.
First run now tells you whether git and a signed-in GitHub CLI are ready for workers' pull requests, with the one command that fixes each, and never blocks Next.
New chat and Project kickoff: files you attach now show above the repository, folder and Runs on row instead of between that row and the input box.

A headless Terminal with Local-first routing on now gets its command forecasts over its device channel, so its capacity broker sizes jobs from what they have needed before. With the flag off it sends nothing, and with no answer it uses its local estimates as before.
With local-first routing on, Auto reserves room on one of your machines when a project starts, goes to Cloud and says why when none has room, and reports what the work actually uses.

Settings → Usage now counts Muse tokens. Models Meta publishes rates for (Muse Wonder 1.0, Spark 1.1–1.3 and the Spark contributor models) are priced at those rates. Models Meta doesn't list, like `muse-wonder-full-1.0-contributor`, show as Unpriced rather than free.
A job in the macOS sandbox shows its output as it prints it, keeps stdout and stderr lines whole, and keeps its exit code when it writes to stderr. Nothing sends work to the sandbox yet.

Muse Personal and Team accounts now appear in Settings → Agents → Accounts, marked Cloud agents only, with usage, Refresh usage, Reconnect and Remove, and they can be added from Add account → Cloud agents. A Local Muse account can be restricted to repositories, as Claude and Codex accounts can. New MCP tools list, switch, pause, restrict, remove and sign in Muse accounts; an agent cannot switch accounts while the active one is at its usage limit.

Kimi workers and Orchestrators keep Claude Code's tool search on when MCP servers connect mid-conversation: the Kimi relay rewrites the `tool_addition` blocks Kimi refuses into tools declared in full, so calls no longer fall back to sending every tool schema.

Signing in with Google, GitHub or Apple now opens your browser or says why it couldn't: the button reads "Opening Google…" until the browser opens, each step fails with a named error within its deadline instead of waiting forever, a "Copy sign-in link" fallback is always there while you wait, and a finished sign-in still reaches a window whose connection to Terminal's local service is down.

The app now calls itself CodePress. Onboarding says "Welcome to CodePress", and the settings, update and error messages, the menu-bar and quit prompts, the window title and the update notices say "CodePress" or "the CodePress app" where they used to say "CodePress Terminal" or "Terminal". Only the words change: the data folder, bundle ID, update feed and `codepress-terminal` tool names stay as they were.

A worker at any provider's limit can continue on another provider's model in one tap. The limit menu holds "Other accounts" and "Other providers" together, leaves out the limited provider's own models, shows a refused model with its reason, and links the provider's own overage page (Claude extra usage, Codex credits, Kimi Extra Usage, Meta's pay-at-limit, xAI Extra Usage Credits) without buying anything.
Three leftover messages now say "the CodePress app" instead of "Terminal": the note about a computer running an older version, the local-connections message, and the installed web app's short name.

Opening a teammate's computer no longer gives it your clipboard or browser. Its window now asks you first, every remote window needs a recent click or key press to open a link, and remote windows only load CodePress and tailnet hosts.
Cloud Orchestrator projects' plan pages now load from Terminal's local server, so they draw with their own styles, scripts and canvas zoom in the desktop app instead of as bare HTML.
Hand off… is listed on every cloud project you can move; the picker says why no Mac can take it.

Pick the Grok account `grok` runs on, in any tab and for any worker: choose one in Settings → Agents → Accounts, and Terminal writes it into `~/.grok`, keeps any tokens the CLI rotates, restarts open conversations one at a time, and puts your own login back when you clear it. A repository rule can bind a repository to an account without moving the rest of the computer, an account can be restricted to repositories, and another computer can show and change this one's choice. With no account chosen, `~/.grok` is never touched.

With local-first routing on, a project with two repositories stays on this machine when your Macs are full instead of going to Cloud with only the first one, and a retried start no longer leaves a second reservation held until the sweep.
The Land dialog can be closed while a land is in flight: Cancel reads Close, Escape and the backdrop dismiss, and the land keeps going in the background.
Preferences → General → Appearance has a Unified view switch. Off opens Terminal's classic title bar and sidebar on this account, and it follows the same choice as the web.
Links open again from an "open another machine" window: outside the desktop app's own window, an external link opens through the window's browser handoff instead of doing nothing.
Landing an Orchestrator project with nothing done (no work items, or every item cancelled) now closes its plan issue as not planned instead of completed.

The Linux arm64 CLI can now be built on an x86 machine: its release build cross-compiles the native parts and checks the packaged arm64 binaries under emulation, with the same glibc requirement as before.

Landing a project, from the Land dialog or the Land answer, now answers as soon as the land commits. Stopping the Orchestrator and workers, closing tabs, removing worktrees and closing issues continue in the background and report in the cleanup post.

Kickoff: with the device URLs flag on, Start and Talk wait while the Orchestrator's model is on a provider this computer is signed out of, beside the note and Open Accounts. Picking a signed-in model or signing in clears it at once.

A synced copy of another Mac's Orchestrator project now shows one conversation-map dash per prompt you sent as soon as the thread opens, and clicking a dash for an older message jumps straight to it in one read, instead of waiting for you to scroll up to the page that holds it. Both Macs need this release, and the backend must support it.

Retire My Work, Design and Servers in Terminal: the rail shortcuts follow the visible rail (Agent ⌃1, Terminal ⌃2, Apps ⌃3, Automations ⌃4, Media ⌃5, Evals ⌃6; Alt+digit off macOS), and links, notifications and in-page navigation to those sections, Coordination or Done open Agent. A custom shortcut saved for a retired section is kept but does nothing.

A Kimi agent at its usage limit now says which limit it hit (5-hour, weekly, or monthly) and when it resets. It waits on the same account and resumes by itself at the reset. A person can switch this computer to another Kimi account from the limit strip. Kimi's concurrent-request, too-many-requests and overload errors are not treated as limits.

Apps page (collections view): an App's preview or widget card no longer reloads when the collections, a collection's members or Loose apps are read again; a card still reloads for a new build, a readiness change or a link near expiry.

Cloud chats in Terminal have an Artifacts view next to Thread: the chat's files, design packets and attachments as a preview-card grid, each opening full size in place. Design packets run in a sandbox that cannot reach the network. A file the agent uploads shows in the thread as a card whose Open jumps to it in Artifacts.

The MCP sign-in card and its composer chip now show on every device that reads a project or chat. On another device they list the servers and their states and say to sign in from Terminal on the home computer, or that it is offline; Not now works from there too.
Make Terminal's macOS release signing of the dictation helper try again when Apple's timestamp service briefly refuses a request, instead of failing the whole arm64 release build.

First run with device URLs on: in the desktop app, signing in to CodePress is the first step (with Continue locally as the way past it), and the signed-in step shows this computer's URL. Signing in on a desktop turns the URL on by itself unless the person turned it off. Off by default behind `terminal_device_urls`.

A signed-out window no longer shows the Agent · Cloud · Terminal switcher or the status bar around the sign-in page. "Use Terminal without signing in" opens Terminal, and its title bar has a Sign in button. Signing in now opens the unified view on Agent, including for an account with no organization, which gets Agent, Terminal and Settings.
Keep Terminal's shared browser network status labels aligned with the live browser route button and refresh its UI dependency manifest.

The Orchestrator's Terminal view now shows the project's worktrees in a row of their own (the session's, then one per worker, named after its work item) above the selected worktree's tabs, on this Mac's projects and on another Mac's. Each worktree remembers the tab you left it on, a worker's terminal link opens on that worker's worktree, and **+** opens a tab in the selected worktree.

With device URLs on, Skip on a Mac permission step (first run or What changed) no longer turns on Computer Use, Remote Desktop or Keep Awake: stored values stay as they are, and What changed does not come back. Finish still saves the switches shown. Off by default behind `terminal_device_urls`.

Shared computers: a teammate's Orchestrator and agents now start when this Mac's Terminal runs on a dynamically linked Node such as Homebrew's. The root helper (version 6) stages the libraries that Node loads from beside itself, and checks the staged Node runs before publishing it. Such a computer is asked to prepare again once.

First run with device URLs on: once you're signed in, the You're Ready step shows how to open this computer on your phone. In the desktop app it shows a QR code of this computer's URL once the URL is connected, plus the CodePress Mobile App Store link. While the URL is still connecting, the step shows the link and says the computer appears in the app once it connects. Off by default behind `terminal_device_urls`.

A worker that hits a limit Terminal can't switch accounts past can now continue by itself on one model you pick ahead of time. Settings → Accounts → "Continue on another provider at a limit" is off by default. Nothing moves to another account, and a destination that is also at its limit, or that a repository rule refuses, means the worker waits, with the reason in the Orchestrator's inbox. The project composer shows "continued on <model>", with Back once the limit resets. Gemini is offered only on an API key, marked per token, never on your own `agy` sign-in.

Tabs whose terminal broker dies while Terminal keeps running (for example, killed by the system when memory runs out) now restart with a fresh shell in place, in their saved folder, with their Claude Code or Codex conversation resumed. Ghostty tabs come back as Ghostty when the setting allows. Before, those tabs stayed stuck until the app was restarted.

Connect my devices: when Device URLs are turned on for your account, Terminal starts no public tunnel until you turn on Connect my devices in Remote Access. With it on, this computer keeps one URL and comes back to it after sleep or a restart. Remote Access shows when you are at your plan's computer limit, when your plan doesn't include a URL for this computer, or when Device URLs are full and Terminal is retrying. With Device URLs off, Remote Access works as before.

The Orchestrator build panel's ⋯ menu now sets how the panel starts (Last used, Open or Closed), the same setting as Settings → Orchestrator. Picking one applies the next time a project opens and leaves the panel in front as it is.
Opening a cloud project in the Orchestrator no longer makes its header jump: Hand off… is listed from the first frame, while the project's record is still loading, instead of appearing once it lands.

With the `terminal_device_urls` flag on, Terminal draws the side nav signed out too: Agent and Terminal on the rail, Settings at its foot, the CodePress mark on the org tile, and a Sign in button in place of the account menu. Settings opens on This computer and offers Sign in. A sign-in keeps the same chrome and the short rail until the account's organizations are known. With the flag off, nothing changes.

You can now sign in to an MCP server from any device that shows the sign-in card or chip. Sign in opens the server's sign-in page in the home computer's agent browser, and Open live browser lets you finish it from the device you are on. Cancel, Try again and Don't ask again work from there too. The sign-in link and tokens stay on the home computer.
A cloud Orchestrator project that could not start now says why in its thread and header, for example "Add a card to start…" with an Open Billing button, instead of reading only as failed.

CodePress Pro upgrade: when the Pro wall is on, Settings, Remote Access and the tunnel window offer Pro ($20/month for 10 computers and custom URLs) to people at the free limit or asking for a custom URL. The mobile app shows no purchase flow, and once checkout completes the app notices without a restart.
Another device can ask this computer to open a terminal in an Orchestrator project, in a chosen worktree. The project's terminals list now says which worktree each one belongs to.
Add the local per-chat artifact store and its owner-only list and content routes. Nothing is visible yet: no tool or Artifacts tab publishes into it until a later release.

Test-only: the macOS actor-helper root test now reads `sshd -T` keywords case-insensitively, because the OpenSSH in macOS 27 prints `DenyUsers` where macOS 15 printed `denyusers`. The installed helper is unchanged.
A cloud project's Hand off picker now lists the Mac you are using (This Mac) the way the web does; it was missing because Terminal's own feed dropped the fields the picker needs.

A computer chat started from the web can carry its referenced context and the app it came from as data. The first message keeps exactly what was typed and shows a "From <app>" chip, and the Orchestrator reads the context as reference data. Terminal advertises `kickoff_context` so the web sends these fields only to a Terminal that takes them.

Every empty or closed Terminal tab now has a Start a terminal button. On another computer's project it opens a shell on that computer, in the selected worktree; a closed or landed local session starts a new one; and "+" opens one more remotely too.

Automatic account switching at a usage limit is now a choice, off by default. Agents wait at the limit and resume at their account's reset. You can turn on "Always switch accounts automatically" from the limit strip or Settings → Agent accounts, after reading the provider's terms. On a tab that uses this computer's active account, a healthy account in the strip now reads "Switch this computer to <account>".

First run, with device URLs on: signing in lands on "Set up your workspace", which joins a workspace you were invited to (or whose email domain is yours) or creates "<First name>'s workspace", so the side nav works from the first minute. This computer's URL moved onto that step. Signing in later from Settings with no workspace shows the step once per account, as a dialog. Local Orchestrator projects made before you had a workspace stay in the feed.

A managed PR review that fails before posting now reaches the delivering agent instead of leaving it waiting. The Factory reports a `review-failed` requirement with the `retry-review` command when the backend's failure marker is on the PR at the current head, and Terminal tells the agent's tab that the review failed and how to re-request it.

Agent tabs and Chat-mode chats get an Artifacts tab. A local agent publishes a report, screenshot, CSV, PDF or HTML mockup with the new `publish_artifact` tool, and it shows as a preview card that opens full size, without a reload. The tab is always there; before anything is published it says how artifacts get there.

Pro upgrade: the checkout watch now keeps running when Settings reloads, so a computer refused at the plan's limit connects on its own once Pro is active. Settings → Network shows one Pro card, under the computer-limit notice, and drops the Quick Tunnel copy while Connect my devices is on.

With Device URLs on, signing in to Terminal on a desktop now turns this computer's URL on by itself when you have never chosen, as first-run intended. An explicit off still stays off. First run no longer falls back to the old order when your plan doesn't include a URL: the panel says so, in the same words as Settings.

Kimi can now switch accounts automatically at a usage limit, if you choose it. Off by default. Turn on "Always switch Kimi accounts automatically" in Settings → Agent accounts or from a Kimi worker's limit strip, after reading Kimi's guideline. Kimi's account is chosen for the whole computer, so a switch moves every Kimi agent on it; the worker restarts on the new account and resumes its session. With no other usable Kimi account it waits for the reset, as before. Kimi accounts restricted to some repositories, or set to cloud agents only, are no longer offered as this computer's Kimi account.
The macOS release builds retry the FFmpeg source download when ffmpeg.org resets the connection, instead of failing the build on the first reset.

An agent tab on another of your machines now shows that machine's Artifacts. In the other-machine agent view the switch gains Artifacts, and a live tab from another Mac gets the same Terminal | Artifacts switch as this Mac's tabs. Files up to 10 MB open full size; larger ones say to open them on that machine. A machine on an older CodePress says to update it.
Copy files an agent publishes in a cloud-synced tab to that tab's CodePress Cloud chat, so the web chat's Artifacts tab lists them.
A Terminal update that hands a local Orchestrator session to the new runtime no longer writes a thread line announcing the move. The conversation still resumes with its history.

A failed managed-review notice for a PR head the branch has already moved past is now shown as informational, without telling the agent to run `retry-review`, so an outdated failure no longer spends the automatic retry.
Add a local-only MCP tool that writes a backend access token directly into a private env file without exposing its value to agents.

Handing a project off to another Mac now shows why that Mac refused, even when the retry replays the stored result. When the reason was not kept, the dialog says so instead of showing the raw receipt.

With the unified view on, the icon rail's Hide list button and ⌘\ now fold the Agent list too, so every section folds its list from the same place. The Agent list's header no longer has its own Collapse sidebar button, and a folded Agent list is hidden completely instead of leaving a slim strip.
Ghostty tabs now blink the cursor when the app asks for it (focused active tab only), lift low-contrast text to a 4.5:1 ratio like xterm tabs, and re-measure the grid after web fonts finish loading.

Local Orchestrator workers now get the project's plan pages: at launch and relaunch Terminal copies each live page into the worker's own temp folder and lists them in its brief under a Designs section, with each page's title, key, size and viewport.

Orchestrator rail: a clicked row is highlighted at once, and a project on another computer opens even when Terminal restored its sign-in at launch. A failed open resyncs and retries once by itself, then says why with Retry, and every click logs how its open ended.

Onboarding's Welcome now shows only the selected Mode card as selected (focus starts on Get Started, and the cards are a radiogroup with arrow keys), and the sign-in step lists what needs a CodePress account and what works without one.

Send in the Orchestrator or Chat kickoff now opens the new thread right away, with your brief as its first message and where it is starting, and the real thread takes over in place once it syncs. No more Sending spinner, "Opening its thread…" or "It is in the agent list."

Plan pages, videos, images and PDFs no longer stay blank when the media signing request never answers: signing gives up after 3 seconds and loads the plain URL, and windows whose daemon isn't enforcing media capabilities stop asking for a signature on every frame.
Ghostty tabs now play the terminal bell and honor OSC 52 clipboard writes and reads, matching xterm tabs. Each effect fires once for live output and never on reload, reattach or history.

A project handoff no longer stays stuck on a failed worker. A failed worker with nothing running in its tab moves as failed history. One whose tab still runs a process blocks with a message naming it and saying how to clear it, and `project_worker_stop` now stops that process and records the worker stopped. A failed worker whose tab is in another Terminal window, or not yet restored, blocks until it can be checked. A handoff refused by an in-flight worker message or restart now says so, instead of listing finished workers.

Each plan page copied for a local Orchestrator worker now gets a PNG screenshot next to it, rendered at the page's declared width in viewport-height tiles, so a worker with image support sees the intended screen without starting a browser.
Feed filter menu: each section with entries behind Show all (Machine with Workspaces, Agent, Repository) now has its own search box, so you can find and tick a match in place.

Terminal no longer carries test coverage for the retired `*.vercel.codepress.dev` web previews: the CodePress web app now runs only on CodePress Apps, so cloud sign-in tokens go to the codepress.dev origin the view opened, as before.
Ghostty tabs now show in split panes, the Orchestrator's quick terminal pane and a work item's Terminal view. Before, their terminal stayed put and those surfaces were empty.
Skip Terminal's integration CI job when its selected plan contains no tests.

A window's live-update streams to its daemon (cards, the PM thread, talk, subagent transcripts) now share one connection, so plan pages, media signing and API calls no longer wait behind them when several Orchestrator views or windows are open. A daemon without the shared stream keeps a connection per stream.

When the Orchestrator relinks a design issue with a reason, Terminal now re-copies the project's plan pages for the item's running workers and the update names the folder (and any page that could not be copied). The Orchestrator's standing prompt now has it name each item's pages in its child issue and treat mockups as an approximate guide, reviewed against intent rather than pixels.

Show a notice when the free Individual plan's 3-computer limit refuses this computer, with Manage computers, Upgrade and Dismiss buttons, stop retrying registration, and show "Individual — N of 3 computers" on the Settings plan line.

Ghostty tabs scroll like xterm tabs: an overlay scrollbar you can click or drag (hidden in full-screen apps), the "New output below ↓" button, the Scroll Speed setting with Alt for fast scroll, and mouse-wheel scrolling in `less` and `man`. Ghostty tabs also keep the full scrollback depth you set, apply Scrollback changes live, show the full-screen-app indicator in the tab bar, and mark background tabs with new output.

Ghostty tabs now support mouse selection: drag, double-click for a word and triple-click for a line, with the selection highlighted. ⌘C, Ctrl+Shift+C, the Copy menu item and the browser copy event copy the selected text with wrapped lines joined. Right-click Paste types into Ghostty tabs, bracketed when the app asks for it. When an app turns on mouse reporting (vim, Claude's TUI), clicks, drags and movement are reported to it, and Shift+drag still selects.
A signed-out window no longer opens on codepress.dev's embedded login page: it lands on Terminal, and a link or Cloud page asked for while signed out opens Terminal's own sign-in prompt instead.

Every local Orchestrator project now has an Artifacts tab from its first frame. It lists what the project's Orchestrator and each of its workers publish, closed workers included, with each card labelled "Orchestrator" or "<work item> · worker". The project's Orchestrator can publish deliverables with `publish_artifact`.
