The move can be followed and retried by its id or operation id, and stopped with the new `cancel_orchestrator_handoff`.
A project's own Orchestrator can now move its project to another machine: the move waits for the Orchestrator's turn to end instead of cutting it off, and its status can be read by operation id.

Every answer of the Orchestrator's project handoff tools now says what to do next, and whether the agent does it itself or only the person can. Orchestrators are told they can move any project, including their own, from the machine they are on.

Verification manifests accept a justified `POST_MERGE` row for an effect that can only be observed after merge, such as the Actions tab no longer listing a deleted workflow. The row names the observation and who makes it, stays out of the derived verdict, and may only cover paths under `.github/` or `.changeset/`; `qa-stamp` refuses one that covers anything a local or staging run reaches and says how to proceed. Terminal reads the new `post_merge` count on stamped QA reports.
`resume_orchestrator_handoff_here` now answers a transfer this machine has no record of as `unknown_after_restart`, with the same next step that status, retry and cancel give, instead of `not_found`.
Keep Terminal CI tests selected when the shared ripgrep setup action changes.
Resume runner host capacity when Active clears a backend-requested drain, while preserving existing local/safety drains and automatic recovery after transient starts or cleanup retries.
Install pinned Docker and jq in Linux CI goldens and advertise verified tools so service-container jobs can spill safely to updated hosts.
Preload pinned PostgreSQL/pgvector and Redis images in Linux CI goldens and use verified local content for their service-container pulls.
Preserve the Remote Desktop expiry reason when a streaming session closes, and automatically reconnect with the same display and granted scope at the session cap.
Speed up periodic cleanup activity reads on large stores and add numeric Remote Desktop gate, keyframe, input, decoder and interval event-loop diagnostics.
A teammate's Team project now shows its HTML plan in the Plans tab instead of an `ORIGIN_NOT_ALLOWED` error.

On a teammate's chat or project in the Team feed, the composer under the thread is now a one-line box while you're reading, like My feed's. Click in or start typing and it opens to the full start composer.
The Antigravity CLI (`agy`) that Terminal installs for Gemini workers is now 1.5.3, which includes `agy acp`, the Agent Client Protocol server.

A local Orchestrator running on Muse or Grok now shows its turn live in the thread (tool calls, subagent spawns and waits, text) instead of "Starting a chat…" for the whole turn. The window no longer checks the Orchestrator's provider against a list of names, and a running turn stays visible even when the PM status cannot be read.
Live browser: the picture no longer freezes when a sign-in redirects the tab to another site while the Chrome window on this machine is minimized.

A teammate's Team chat or project header is tidier: Add to my feed and Send to… are smaller, the Continue in my own chat button is gone (start your own chat from the composer under the thread with Start my own chat or Start my own Orchestrator project), the Read-only chip is gone (you can message the owner's agent), and the owner shows with their profile picture, or the same initials and colors they have in the Team feed.
The Grok Orchestrator's ACP session is now a shared engine, with a Gemini session on `agy acp` built on it. Nothing calls the Gemini session yet, and the Grok Orchestrator behaves the same.
Edge relay: a request that reaches this computer during a short daemon freeze now gets its late answer instead of a 502 `terminal_unreachable`.
The edge relay connection no longer stalls for 15 seconds when the relay's first message arrives together with its connection reply.
Reduce Desktop stalls from periodic project cleanup by indexing reclaim reads and pruning landed history in bounded batches that yield to the daemon event loop.

Orchestrator: a project's Terminal tab now opens on its newest running worker's agent terminal, in that worker's worktree, instead of the idle Session shell, until you pick a tab. With no worker running it opens on the Session shell as before, and a tab you pick stays picked.

Every chat and project is now Team or Personal, so the "Who should see your older chats and projects?" card in the feed and the matching row in Preferences are gone, and a project's menu no longer shows a "Not shared with your team yet" state.
A teammate's Team chat or project now opens its composer on Message <first name>'s agent instead of Start my own chat. Starting your own chat or project is still one pick away in the same Send menu.

Pressing a machine's green "Connected here" icon in the Machines picker now disconnects that machine from this Terminal. It shows a spinner until the connection closes, shows any error on the row, and sends this window back to this machine if the disconnected one was selected.
Update the Claude Agent SDK to 0.3.321, shipping Claude Code 2.1.321 for local Orchestrator and local-device agent sessions. Claude Fable 5.2 runs without an unrecognized-model warning.
Offer Claude Fable 5.2 in place of Fable 5.1 in the model pickers, and price Fable 5.2 usage at $8 / $40 per million tokens ($0.20 cache reads, $10 / $16 cache writes).
Disconnect another machine automatically once no window on screen has shown any of its tabs for 5 minutes, so forgotten connections stop pinging it.
App reads ask the backend for path-mode preview URLs, so App frames load in Terminal on WebKit and when Terminal is open in a Chromium browser tab.
Settings → App hosting and Team computers now draw in Terminal's Settings pane instead of loading the web page. App hosting's billing link still opens Billing in the embedded web view.

The local Orchestrator can now run on the Antigravity CLI (`agy acp`), behind the scenes for now: Gemini is not yet offered in the Orchestrator's model picker. It runs on a repository rule's Gemini key, this machine's chosen key, agy's own API key, or your Google sign-in, in that order, and says what to do when none can serve. A key never reaches the agent: it goes through Terminal's relay. A sign-in Orchestrator never gets your Gemini key from Terminal's environment. A Google rate limit on a key fails the turn with the agent's words, and the Orchestrator is never moved to another key or account.
Reconnect Desktop sessions automatically after short relay outages while the host status is unavailable or its display is waking.

A teammate's message to a project or chat on this machine now brings the files they attached: Terminal downloads them, puts them on the teammate's post in the thread, saves them where the Orchestrator reads them and lists them in its inbox entry. A file that cannot be fetched is named as missing and the rest still arrive.

Message <owner>'s agent under a teammate's Team chat or project now takes files: the `+`, paste and drop attach files that upload first and go with your words, and the tray survives the composer folding and the Work panel opening.
Avoid repeating frontend and server preparation during Turbo desktop builds while retaining upstream workspace builds.
The Orchestrator answers a question about an existing plan in the thread instead of editing the plan, and revises it only when you ask for a change or accept its offer.
Add Terminal's App chat host (`useTerminalAppChat`) and its launch confirm card, ready for the App page to run its chat natively. Not routed yet, so nothing changes on screen.

Connect a Google subscription to Gemini with one button. Accounts → Google, onboarding and a signed-out Gemini model entry now offer Sign in with Google, Gemini Enterprise and Sign in with a code for a machine with no browser. Google's own agent runs the sign-in, and Terminal never sees the token. A signed-in row shows the plan, and Sign out uses agy's own sign-out.
Words typed while a plan approval card is open now reach the Orchestrator as an ordinary message, and the card stays open. Only pressing "Ask for changes" records a change request.

Settings → Connections, Usage and Branding are drawn in Terminal's Settings modal instead of the embedded web page. Branding's logos upload from Terminal and show on white in both themes. Terminal's backend client now sends file uploads as multipart form data.
The local Orchestrator now says each answer once: after posting it no longer repeats the post in its closing reply, and a later turn no longer re-answers a question it already answered.

The Claude Orchestrator now starts with only its six core project tools loaded (snapshot, update, post and the inbox) and loads the others through tool search when it first needs them, taking about 30k tokens off every request. Tool search is on for every Orchestrator launch, whatever account it signs in with.

Start chats from a launch in Terminal: Automations' New, and pages that start a chat with instructions and context, show a confirm card, create the chat in Terminal and open it in Agent instead of opening the web's chat page.

A Claude Orchestrator now gets an explicit list of Claude Code built-in tools instead of every default, and Claude's Artifact tool is off unless you turn it on in Account → Orchestrator → Tools (or ask an agent to set `orchestratorClaudeArtifacts`).

Settings → Branding in Terminal now shows the whole section: the brand agent, the dashboard and publishing domains, the installable app with its QR code, the CodePress address, who can join, and ejecting the dashboard, instead of a note pointing to the web.
The file editor's status bar shows the cursor line's git blame beside `Ln, Col`, with a commit card on hover or tap.

Behind Orchestrator for Apps, a local Orchestrator can find the organization's Apps and link its project to the one App it changes (project_app_find, project_app_link). The project's snapshot shows that App and whether each work item takes the App flow, and the synced card tells CodePress which App the project changes.
A Mac that finished sandbox setup restarts Apple's `container` runtime by itself after a reboot, so it keeps taking automations without another click on "Set up this Mac".

Fable 5.2 now runs with a 200k context window everywhere Terminal starts it, on every Claude Code version, because Fable is expensive. To give Fable 5.2 its 1M window, turn on Fable 5.2 · 1M context in Account → Agents (or `claudeLongContext` in the agent settings). The compaction windows show Fable's range to match.
Codex, Muse and Grok Orchestrators no longer see Claude's ToolSearch instruction, and their project tools carry the same core/deferred metadata Claude's do.

The Orchestrator's project tools cost about 40% fewer tokens once loaded: each tool's description now says only what it does, its arguments and its answers, and the rules the Orchestrator's instructions already give are no longer repeated in them. No tool's name or arguments changed.
Restamp the Orchestrator store's schema fingerprint for the `projects.apps_json` column added in #21458, so stores open through the one-time pass and pick it up.

A synced copy of a project homed on another machine now shows git blame in its Files editor: the status-bar item and the end-of-line annotation, asked of the home over the pane relay. An older home shows no blame, as before.
Orchestrator projects saved by an earlier build run the one-time schema pass once more on open, so they pick up the App link column added for Orchestrator for Apps.
Orchestrator: starting a build no longer labels the plan and design issues `cp:in-progress`; they are only assigned to you. Landing still takes the label off issues an earlier build labelled.

Settings → Agents (the list and each agent), Browser profiles and Browser network are drawn natively in Terminal's Settings modal when a link opens them, instead of in the embedded web view. Messaging an agent starts the chat in Terminal.

Orchestrator for Apps: projects get an App tab listing the App they build with Open in CodePress, the kickoff repo picker lists the organization's Apps, and Project settings shows and changes the project's App. Behind the Orchestrator for Apps flag.

Model menus now have a Context section whenever Fable 5.2 is selected: choose 200k (the default) or 1M right there, and the chip shows "· 1M" while it is on. It is the same account setting as Account → Agents, so a change in either shows in the other, and it applies to agents started afterwards.
CI test selection: a ci.yml edit runs the Terminal Vitest and Rust suites in full only when it reaches their jobs.

Rename any of your machines from the machine menu: hover a name to see it as a field, click it (or press Enter or F2) to edit it in place, then Enter to save or Esc to cancel. Clicking a name no longer connects; the terminal icon still does, and this machine's row shows it while you are driving another machine so you can come back.

Shared UI for Orchestrator for Apps on the web App page: an embedded mode for the Agents feed, a step strip, and an Open plan button on plan approval where a host offers one. Terminal draws nothing new.

Repair local fast builds on Linux with a debug AppImage, retain the macOS debug app bundle, and preserve shared resource preparation without generating updater artifacts. Packaged debug builds use bundled runtime resources and production settings while retaining debug-only service and update policies.

Mac automations Settings: approving "Run my automations" no longer says it failed when the approval stored; the allow-once ask names the automation and says it tried to run here, not that an agent asked; Lima machines say their sandbox keeps jobs off the local network instead of offering the guard; the allow-once notice says the run goes elsewhere, not to the cloud.

Orchestrator for Apps: a local project on the organization's App repository gets an Apps section in its Orchestrator's instructions (steps open PRs into the project's feature branch, the Orchestrator checks the preview before integrating, and the person publishes). The App tab, kickoff Apps and settings App row now stay hidden while Hosted App editing is off. Behind the Orchestrator for Apps flag.

A Gemini Orchestrator now gets its project tools on its first turn. agy declares only a small budget of a session's tools and silently dropped the Orchestrator's core ones, so the Orchestrator now runs one server of its own per session, with the core project tools and a tool_search/tool_call gateway to every other tool, and a failed tool's own error message shows in the thread.
Settings → Members: Invite members opens the invite dialog in Terminal instead of sending you to the web Members page.

The Orchestrator writes times in your time zone instead of UTC. Terminal tells it this machine's time zone (for example `America/Los_Angeles (PST)`) on each turn, so a change reaches it on the next one; on a cloud server or a machine set to UTC it names no zone and labels every time instead.
Settings no longer says "That didn't go through" after turning an allow off worked but its reply was lost while the admin dialog ran; it reads the state again first.

Run a local Orchestrator on Gemini. Kickoff, Project settings and the thread composer now offer Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro for the Orchestrator, running Google's Antigravity agent (`agy acp`) on this machine with your own Google sign-in or a Gemini API key. Each entry says which credential it runs on, or why it can't run, and offers Sign in with Google when you're signed out. Cloud Orchestrators don't offer Gemini.
Apps: Link a site and Add a blog open their dialogs in Terminal, and Migrate a site opens the web's dialog in your browser instead of the embedded web view.

Remote Desktop remembers a machine on this device the first time you connect, so there is no "Trust this host" checkbox or consent sheet any more, and the workbench Desktop view connects by itself when you open it. If a machine later presents a different key, the view stops with "Couldn't confirm this is <machine>", shows both fingerprints, and offers Try again, Pair anyway… or Not now.

Interactions opens in Terminal, with its rail entry wherever the organization has it on, and Automations' Set up GitHub and repository controls work in Terminal: installing a GitHub App opens your browser, and the page refreshes when you come back.
A Gemini Orchestrator that Google stops for quota now says so: the turn fails with Google's message and when the quota resets, instead of looking as if it finished quietly.

Choose your time zone in Account → Preferences → General → Time zone. Automatic, the default, keeps using the time zone of the machine the Orchestrator runs on. A zone you pick applies on every machine and in the cloud, and the Orchestrator writes times in it from its next turn. Agents can read and set it as `timeZone` in `get_terminal_agent_settings` and `update_terminal_agent_settings`.

Settings → Integrations and Platform MCP now draw in Terminal's own Settings window instead of the embedded web page, every provider included. Connecting a provider (Slack, GitHub, an MCP server's sign-in and the rest) opens your system browser, and the page reads again when you come back, so an abandoned connect leaves it as it was and ready to try again. An agent's Integrations tab now draws its providers here too, and WhatsApp's template delete and number release work from Terminal.
A Gemini Orchestrator that names its own tool server when it calls a project tool (such as assigning a worker) now reaches that tool, instead of being told the server doesn't exist.

Open another machine's screen from where your machines live: "View desktop" on each other online machine in the rail's machines menu, and "View desktop: <machine>" in the command palette. Both open a Desktop tab already pointed at that machine in the current Terminal session (starting a session if none is open), or bring back the one already open. Machine rows no longer spell out "Online" / "Offline": the green or grey dot says it, and screen readers still hear it.

Remote Desktop: when CodePress is set up again on a machine and its key changes, the viewer checks the new key with your account and reconnects by itself with a quiet note, instead of asking you to pair again.

The Remote Desktop viewer has one toolbar: the machine (with its power and remote unlock readiness in its menu), the display when there is more than one, a status only while it isn't live, the view controls, one Expand, and a ⋯ menu with Fullscreen, Actual size, Latency HUD, Open in a tab, Connection info, Remote access settings and Disconnect. Connecting, can't reach, key not confirmed, locked, disconnected and no machine each show a centered panel, and Connection info shows the machine's fingerprint with Forget this machine. On a phone the toolbar is the machine, Fit, Keyboard and ⋯, with the rest in a sheet.
Preserve bundled SDK executables during Linux AppImage preparation, and stage node-pty runtime binaries without source-build intermediates.
Reuse verified unsigned runner dependency archives for eligible local desktop builds, with fresh release files and full preparation on cache faults.

Server CLI: after an update, the service now waits up to 60 s (`CODEPRESS_HEADLESS_BROKER_READY_WAIT_MS`) for its selected PTY broker to finish connecting, instead of exiting when the first check finds it between connections. Newly discovered broker generations no longer log a false "Connection to broker closed" or start an extra discovery pass.

Terminal draws a managed App's page itself, with no embedded web page: the
preview, editing, Publish, Settings and the App's chat open at once from
Terminal's own code. A link to a page inside an App opens that page, and the
address Terminal keeps for it is the web's. Hosting, billing, the GitHub
repository picker and a migrated site's card open on the web in your browser.
Linked, repository and default Apps, and Apps in other organizations, still
open in the embedded view.

A personal Server CLI updated from Update all, or once its agents go idle, now finishes the install when its connection to CodePress reconnects during the download or the wait, instead of failing with "Owner authorization changed". If the connection stays down, the update fails with "Lost its connection to CodePress; try again".

Auto's check for another machine's copy of a repository answers in seconds instead of timing out: only that repository's checkouts are read, from the recent scan, and remote reads no longer wait behind remote writes. A machine that is only reconnecting is no longer called outdated or left out of Auto, and a read that times out is logged as a timeout.

Terminal draws linked websites and default apps (Search & SEO, Redirects,
Analytics and the other website tools) itself, with no embedded web page, as
well as an App's Analytics address and the preview of a generated App's pull
request. Writing a linked blog's post opens that post's editor on the web in
your browser; coming back to Terminal shows what you saved. A linked site on
CodePress's own domain, which the web shows live, still opens in the embedded
view, as do repository Apps and agent artifacts.

Choosing a project folder on another machine now keeps working through a brief reconnect, and when that machine still can't be reached the picker says it is reconnecting or didn't answer instead of a generic error.
Preserve Desktop machine-save errors after rollback and ignore failed saves for superseded selections.

A cross-machine message that the backend resends after a restart is typed into the tab once: a Terminal answers a repeated message id with the first delivery's result and advertises `agent_message_dedupe_v1`.

Terminal draws repository Apps, "Host this repo" and agent artifacts itself, with
no embedded web page. A repository App's preview, Start, the change picker,
editing, Save → PR and its chat open from Terminal's own code, and Terminal knows
a preview on this machine without asking the Desktop's loopback. An artifact that
heads a canvas shows its pages, and a link to one page of it opens that page.
"Host this repo" sets up a repository's website in Terminal; connecting a GitHub
App still opens in your browser. A link to another organization's artifact still
opens in the embedded view.

The Orchestrator now writes reports that someone who did not see the work can follow. A worker's brief says how to finish and offers a "Problems seen, not fixed" section in its pull request. The Orchestrator reads those entries from the project snapshot and suggests them as follow-ups when it lands. The bundled delegation skills name a current Codex model.

An automation marked as changed without a person's sign-in now shows a Review and vouch button beside the notice in its Live And Draft panel, so the mark can be cleared even when the draft matches live.

The Orchestrator's designs now list every gate a flagged change ships that ignores the flag, with its way through when the flag is off and the test that proves it, and accept the work only with a test that flag-off behavior is unchanged starting from data already in the new state.

Keep this machine connected through backend restarts: when the backend asks the device channel to move, Terminal opens a new connection and switches to it before closing the old one, so requests to this machine no longer fail during a backend worker recycle or deploy.

The Orchestrator reads its project record with less work: issue links, App lookups and landed conversations read only the fields they use, and each project snapshot reads post questions, open asks and merge results once per read instead of once per row.

The chat docked on an App's page now streams new messages live when the turn was started somewhere else (Agents → Chats, another machine), after the page was hidden and shown again, and when you come back to an App, instead of showing a stale transcript until you reload.
When Terminal can't send the backend its copy of an automation you allowed (no sign-in, device id or organization), it now logs why instead of dropping it silently.

Apps can now add every app found in a connected repository at once with "Add from a repository", and Host this repo's Folder field lists the repository's folders and checks the one you pick (behind the staff Unified Apps flag).

New app now takes you to the App it builds. When the chat started from New app in a collection creates the App, Terminal opens that App's page with the same chat docked beside the preview, instead of leaving you in the Agents chat. A reloaded transcript, a chat you have already left, or a second App made in the same chat does not move you.

The local Orchestrator's project snapshot is now compact and never cut off: settings come first, then the project, open asks, open work items in full, finished items and workers in a short form, and the newest posts. A `work_item` argument reads one item in full.

Show download progress while Terminal installs a worker CLI: the setup strip now reads "Downloading Antigravity CLI · 34 of 65 MB" with a progress bar, then "Unpacking…" and "Verifying…", instead of a plain "Installing…" for the whole download.
Typing @ now lists Chat-mode chats under Chats and projects under Projects, on this machine and your other machines. Older chats that share words with a newer project now show up too.
When Claude declines a request, the turn now fails with one notice that says so and names the category in plain words, instead of finishing with an empty reply.

The `@` menu lists your own cloud and Slack chats under Chats › Cloud. Mentioning one in a message to a project gives the Orchestrator that chat's recent messages as your own words, and a chat that can't be read stops the send with your draft kept.
On a phone, a long `@` menu no longer slides under the "This list may be out of date" banner: its header and Close stay visible and the rows scroll inside it.

A cloud Orchestrator refused because its personal-token repository has no usable GitHub credential now says why once, with an Open GitHub settings button, instead of retrying and reading "It will try again shortly".
Gemini now shows Google's current four-colour spark on a neutral tile in Settings → Account and the worker setup rows, instead of a white spark on a purple tile.

In the unified view, the title bar and icon rail now form one frame with no dividing lines, and the list and page sit together in a card with a rounded top-left corner. Cloud view and browser tabs round the same corner when the list is folded.
A chat that proposes an App plan now shows the plan card in Terminal's chat view, with Approve & build opening the project it starts (staff-only flag).

On macOS 26 and later, CodePress shows the current window controls and window corners. The macOS app is now built with Xcode 26 or later, and the window controls sit centred in the title bar of every window.

Take a Talk call started from the CodePress web page on this machine's Codex Orchestrator: the call joins the Orchestrator's own conversation, its events reach the browser over the live thread stream, and moving a call between a Terminal window and the browser tells the other side the call moved.

Terminal's cloud dictation now uses the multipart body, refusal parsing and cloud-access rule it shares with the web app; dictation behaves as before. The new-chat model chip now truncates its label when the composer row is tight, so its sponsor badge no longer slides under the mic.
Automation settings show the "Needs fixed IP" card when the organization has a fixed egress IP: admins mark an automation as needing it, see the IP to allowlist, and its run location locks to Cloud.
An App's hosting view says how long its builds usually take, and when they are slow it suggests adding the folder with a dev server on this machine.
The Intel macOS build bundles an executable node-pty spawn helper again, so the Intel release build gets past node-pty staging.

The Hand off dialog's check now answers in seconds, even on a busy machine with several workers running. It no longer reads every worker's conversation or opens a login shell for each one, and it stops working as soon as you close the dialog or pick another destination. The move itself runs the same checks as before.

Hand off: choosing a machine makes Hand off usable at once. The pre-move check fills one fixed-height line under the tiles ("Checking the move", a calm line for a busy machine, "Check again" when it gives up), a disabled button says why, tiles line up across a row, the ring starts on the Suggested machine, and arrowing across tiles asks about the last one only.

Hand off: a move no longer freezes Terminal while it prepares. Large conversation transcripts are read, checked and compressed in a background thread, one login shell and one process read serve the whole move, workers are prepared a few at a time, and the server logs each step's time with the longest event-loop delay.

Hand off keeps one dialog frame from the press to the end, names the step under way in progress tense with one elapsed clock, and a failed move gives one reason with Retry and Resume here showing they are working. The thread's hand-off banner keeps one height across its states, its waiting ring no longer looks like a stuck spinner, and the rail says "Moving to …" and "Hand off failed".

When the Terminal daemon exits during start-up, the app now reports it within a fraction of a second, with the exit status and the name of the daemon's error log, instead of waiting out the 30-second start timeout. The previous start's error log is kept as `server-<window>-stderr.log.1` so a restart no longer erases it.
A stopped worker launch queue no longer launches a queued worker, and attaching a pull request no longer pauses Terminal's server while it reads the repository's remote.

Terminal now checks the Node.js runtime it downloads against a pinned SHA-256 from nodejs.org before unpacking or running it, and refuses an archive that does not match while keeping the existing runtime. Unpacking and starting the server no longer run on the app's async worker threads, and staging folders left behind by a crashed download are cleaned up after an hour.

The sign-in token, signed-in user and telemetry storage keys are now defined once and shared by every part of Terminal that reads them. Nothing changes for you: the values are the same, so you stay signed in and your telemetry choice is kept after the update.

Terminal's local windows no longer hold the process, store and updater plugin permissions or the shell spawn and execute permissions, none of which they used. Opening links and installing updates work as before.

Updates: when replacing the app needs an administrator password, the installed app is moved aside rather than deleted first, and put back if the new one cannot be moved in, so a failed install no longer leaves the machine without Terminal. Installing a chosen version refuses a malformed version before downloading anything, staging an update no longer holds up other work while another Terminal stages the same version, and on Linux a leftover update download whose process id now belongs to another program is cleaned up.

New project and Chat: the Team/Personal chip now also shows when Runs on is another of your machines, and the chat or project starts there with what you picked. Machines whose CodePress app is too old to keep it look and work as before.

Daemon recovery: when Terminal replaces a daemon that still answers, it now waits for that daemon to finish its own cleanup (previews, runners, the Orchestrator host) before force-stopping it, and a daemon adopted from an earlier run is stopped instead of being left running beside its replacement. An adopted daemon is stopped only once Terminal has confirmed it is this window's daemon. Its health endpoint can confirm that; when it does not answer, its command line, the window and data folder it was started for, and a start time no later than its pid file confirm it instead. A wedged daemon is still stopped at once.
Retry a dictation once by itself after a network or server failure, and keep the clip with a Retry button if it still fails.

When this computer's device signing key is unavailable, Terminal now says why (for example another CodePress process was still setting the key up, or its key file is damaged), logs and reports the cause once, and retries once after a short wait when the key's lock was still held.
The agent feed now shows each row's latest activity time in Planning and Working, so a project still planning on this machine no longer reads hours old while its Orchestrator keeps working.

Look for set-aside work once per machine instead of once per synced project: one request a minute for the whole machine, plus an immediate look when the cloud says set-aside work arrived. Falls back to the per-project reads against a backend without the batched route.

The Orchestrator's plans now prove per-screen layout and phone-width criteria with QA evidence (a screenshot and a box measurement taken in the QA run) instead of a new browser test, and ask for a browser end-to-end test only for a new or changed core user flow. The Factory init bundle's frontend-qa and qa-verifier guidance keeps layout probes outside the ordinary end-to-end suite.
A computer running Terminal now accepts an update check or install request from its owner's web or phone session, through the existing remote-control relay, for the Terminal update tools only.
A managed App's change preview in Terminal reads live data and refuses writes, as on the web.

Project sync makes far fewer background requests. A machine now keeps one answer per organization for its sync settings, shared by every window, the one feed and the move picker. Callers that ask while a read is out wait for it instead of sending their own. An organization whose settings are refused (401, 403 or 404) is asked again after 30 seconds rather than on every check; any other failed read is retried on the next check, as before. The repair pass also reads and lists only the organizations where this machine has a project or a cloud copy. An account in many organizations used to read every one of them about once a minute. A settings change is still seen at once, and organizations with projects here are repaired as often as before.
Remove nine native commands nothing calls, four unused H.264 encoder methods and the unused process and store plugins.
Remove unused Terminal server code: the unwired browser-profile authority core and journal, two synchronous git helpers, two factories with no callers, and test-only wrapper exports.

Signed-out windows always have the side nav and open on the sign-in screen. Terminal stays one press away ("Use Terminal without signing in", or the rail), and a window where you chose Terminal keeps opening there. The Unified view switch is now in This computer → General while signed out, so you can turn the classic layout on or back off without an account.
Idle Orchestrator session folders are reclaimed through the shared saved-worktree module; the old session-only copy is removed.

Evals in Terminal's shell now set up an eval in plain words. The new-eval form offers four kinds of target (agent or skill, CodePress automation, your code, HTTP endpoint), and a kind the server cannot run says why. The suite's Review tab is now Setup and explains what runs, what each case gets and what counts as right. Runs of an automation, command or endpoint take a version, branch or base URL.

Internal: the server tests are now typechecked in CI against a baseline that only shrinks, and React's rules of hooks are linted. Helper functions that were named like hooks were renamed; behavior is unchanged.
Drop the server-test type baseline entry for the deleted session-saved-worktree test, so the Terminal typecheck ratchet passes again.

Remove dependency declarations nothing imports. Terminal drops `@tauri-apps/plugin-process`, whose native plugin was already removed. The engine drops the devDependencies `@babel/plugin-syntax-jsx` and `supertest`, which only its own tests could have used and none do, so the published engine's code and runtime dependencies are unchanged.
Terminal's sidebar, tab and workflow lists now use the one shared drag-to-reorder list from the UI package instead of a separate copy. Dragging behaves as before.

Test tooling only: the retired `agent-settings-live` Playwright spec (every case skipped since #18499) and its config are deleted, and Terminal's e2e selector no longer lists it. No change to the app.

Manage hosting in Terminal's shell has a Previews tab for a site with source builds on. Turn on a preview link for every pushed branch, choose whether only your team or anyone with the link can open them, and copy, open or delete each branch's link. A failed branch build shows its error and its build logs.

Remove unused Terminal UI code: the duplicate terminal context menu component, three hooks and an OAuth helper nothing imported, and about thirty exports with no caller. The right-click Copy action in the terminal keeps its test. No behaviour changes.

Internal: removed unused icon sets (Android, iOS, design concepts and Windows Store logos), the unused build/entitlements.mac.plist, the tracked build/icon.iconset copy that the release scripts regenerate, and two unreferenced scripts. The app bundle icons are unchanged.
Settings → My computers in Terminal is unchanged: the update state and Update buttons added for the web and phone (#22073) are not shown here.

Terminal no longer runs a machine-wide cloudflared process sweep at startup. That sweep only matched an old checkout layout, so it never found anything in installed builds. Startup still stops a leftover tunnel through its saved process ID.

Remove unused shared UI code from packages/ui (the retired slim project rail, unused exports and export-map entries, and a duplicate relative-time helper). Terminal looks and behaves the same; only its build's list of shared UI source files changes.
Remove an unused helper from the subscription accounts settings code. Nothing changes for people using Terminal.

Evals: the Setup tab shows which model the setup agent runs on. When the agent's turn fails, the tab shows the error with Try again. "Set up with agent" now explains why it cannot start when no Codex credential can run it, with a link to connect one.
A chat's Dock now shows secret request cards ("Allow a secret to go to …?", "Add a secret"), as a project's does, so a chat that asks for a secret can be answered from its thread.
The desktop title bar's first item now starts 16px clear of the macOS window controls, and the whole row (title, tabs, chips, search, update pill) centres on the same line as the controls.
Keep the main window's traffic lights centred in the title bar on macOS 26 and later. They no longer jump to the top edge after the window redraws.
Managed automation settings show readable labels and fitting controls, and the repository policy shows the organization values it inherits.
Edge relay: a daemon whose event loop stalls for a few seconds stays attached instead of dropping a live relay socket, and a 1006 drop now logs the socket error behind it.
The managed automation dialog has a compact header, Setup, Rules, Repository overrides and Activity tabs, and one save footer that says when changes are unsaved.

Remote Desktop: each Desktop connect now writes one `[RemoteDesktop] connect timing` line to the Terminal log with the time of each step (status read, start, first frame, total) and whether it went through the native app or the webview, and the viewer's Copy stats shows its own status, ticket, handshake and first-frame times. The status-read, socket-closed and session-end lines now reach the log file too.

Desktop viewer: when you connect to a machine that is slow to answer, the viewer no longer stops at "The machine didn't answer… then refresh". It keeps checking every few seconds for up to 30 seconds and connects as soon as the machine answers, showing "Waiting for {machine} to answer…" with an attempt count and a Stop trying button. While connecting, the panel now says which step it is on: checking the machine, starting the screen, or waiting for the picture.

The WhatsApp settings page in Terminal now shows a first-run card when your workspace has no number, lists numbers as rows with one status sentence and a ⋯ menu, and gives workspace members a read-only view with a prompt to link their phone instead of admin actions.

Remote Desktop status reads are answered by the native app in milliseconds, so a machine whose window is in the background or whose display is asleep no longer times out with "The machine didn't answer". An older app without the new route keeps the previous webview read.

The project owner's other devices can answer an Orchestrator's secret card: the home machine checks each answer against CodePress with its own person login before the Orchestrator hears it. Closing a card without deciding no longer tells the Orchestrator never to ask again.

Plan pages can now be saved after a hand edit (the Edit mode that uses this comes next): the save checks the page has not changed since the edit began, keeps its link, and tells the Orchestrator, which reads the edited page before it publishes that page again instead of overwriting it.
The composer's lock button is gone from the toolbar: Add a secret is now in the + menu, right after Attach file.

Opening a machine's screen while it is unlocked now starts capture in the native app instead of waiting on the app's window, which macOS can slow down for up to 10 seconds when it is minimized or in the background. Live resizing works on these sessions, and a start that sends no picture within 4 seconds, or an older app, falls back to the previous start.

For people served the new onboarding, the app's first run now follows their account after sign-in. Someone already in a finished workspace sees it named on Connect. Someone with an invitation joins first. Someone with no workspace names one, connects accounts, and picks what to do first; Start finishes the workspace's setup. Setup progress is saved on the workspace, so a half-done setup resumes where it stopped, on the web or in the app. Everyone else's first run is unchanged.

WhatsApp settings: adding a number now opens a guided setup page instead of a dialog. It asks who will message the number (your team or your customers) and where the number comes from (a new number or one you already have), shows a summary with the price to check, and then connects the number on the same page. Provider and Meta terms appear only under "Advanced options". Back, Forward and reload keep your place.

For people served the new onboarding, Add workspace in the app's workspace switcher now creates another workspace right in the app and walks you through its setup: name it, check your accounts, then pick what to do first. The app switches to the new workspace as soon as it exists. Close the setup at any step with ✕ or Escape; the workspace then shows "Setup not finished" in the switcher, and picking it reopens the setup where you left off. Everyone else's switcher and Add workspace are unchanged.

The project's owner can answer an Orchestrator's secret cards (Allow, Save, Use a saved secret) from a copy of the project on another machine, the web app or a phone. The change is saved to CodePress under their own login from that device, and the project's machine checks it there before telling the Orchestrator. The card says where the choice goes, what Dismiss leaves undecided, and links to the secret's access in Settings.

Settings now shows an automation asking to run on this machine the moment it asks: it waits at the top of the CodePress app page under "Waiting for you" with an Allow button, and the CodePress app item in the Settings list shows how many are waiting. An allowed automation's row keeps its name instead of turning into its id.

For people served web onboarding v2, the app's full setup now includes web v2's Connect GitHub, Choose a plan and Invite your team steps, between Connect your accounts and the permission screen. Team checkout opens in the browser, and the app confirms the plan when the person comes back. A draft saved on one of these steps resumes on it. Nobody outside the flag sees a change.

When an automation tried to run on this machine and went to the cloud, Terminal now shows a notification and a card in the main window naming it, with one Allow button that opens the password or Touch ID dialog. Notifications are limited to one per automation a day and pause for a week after Decline.

Plans: an Edit toggle on the plan canvas lets you change a plan page's text, duplicate, move or delete its blocks, and save the page, with a prompt when the Orchestrator published a newer version meanwhile.

Replay onboarding: people served the new onboarding can walk the app's onboarding again from Settings → General (full setup on a test workspace, already set up, or invited), as often as they like, without changing their real first run. Test workspaces are listed in the chooser and can be deleted.
Add workspace: reopening an unfinished workspace from the switcher now always opens on the step its setup was saved on, instead of sometimes going back to Name.

Design kit: page sources. A `pages.source` name lets two configs capture pages into one kit without erasing each other: a capture rewrites only its own source's frames, rows and gap rows, writes its stylesheet to `css/routes--<source>.css`, and fails with exit 2 naming both sources when a page name is already captured by another. Page hooks can return `beforeReady`, which runs once the shell shows and before the page's ready selector. Terminal's own windows (workspace, Settings, an Orchestrator project) are now captured into CodePress's kit with `pnpm design-kit:pages`; nothing in Terminal's app changes.
The `@` menu opens above the line on a phone while the keyboard is up, instead of two rows tall under the input.

Apps connected to a repository get an Environment variables section in Settings: see and edit public values, keep secrets hidden, paste a .env file, choose where each variable applies, and redeploy when saved variables differ from the live release. Manage hosting's Settings now links there.

Plan pages in Edit mode: drag any element by its handle to a new place in the page, shown by a drop line, or hold Alt/Option (or use Place freely) to put it at an exact spot. Reset position takes a placement back, and each move undoes like any other edit.

WhatsApp settings: the last step of adding a number is now a checklist that shows where setup is (reserved, verified, connected to WhatsApp, able to send) with the buttons for the current step, such as Sign in with Facebook, Try again or Cancel setup. Errors stay in their row until you dismiss them. You can leave the page while setup carries on: a "Finish setting up" card above your numbers takes you back. If you back out of the Facebook sign-up, the page says so and keeps your setup.

Settings → My computers now sends computer updates through the shared update code that the web's machine menu also uses. Nothing changes in Terminal: its My computers page and machine menu look and behave as before, and the update badge stays in the title bar.
WhatsApp settings: disconnecting a number now asks for confirmation and says whether the number is released for good, and paused numbers show why and how to turn them back on.

Plans: while editing a plan page, a Page / HTML switch shows the page's HTML source beside a live preview (full width on a phone, with a Preview toggle), so you can add sections, fix markup or paste HTML; Save sends the source exactly as typed.

Settings → CodePress app now lists the automations running on this machine under "Run my automations on this machine", with how long each has run and the last few that ended, each with a link to open it on the web. The CodePress app item in the Settings list shows a small dot while one runs.
Download is offered for a project's large artifacts again, with progress, a failure and Retry, and a ⋯ menu for previous, next and full screen on a narrow gallery.
Plan canvas: in Edit mode, drag a plan page by its label to a new spot. The move is saved at once, shows on the plan's share link, and the Orchestrator's later publishes keep the person's position.

Settings groups now read You, Organization and "This computer · <name>", and every Settings page shows who owns it with a chip beside its title ("You · follows you", "Organization · set by admins", "This computer · <name>"), with each page's title shown once. The note on Agent accounts saying which choices follow you is readable again in light and dark themes. Messages that pointed to Settings → Account or Computer now name the new groups. Long machine names truncate in the Settings rail.

Apps: a new default app, CI runners, can be added from Default apps. It shows your CI machines, the live queue, where each job ran and why, and what running on your own machines saved. Organizations that have not connected a CI machine see how to connect one, and admins can create a reporter token and enter prices there. An app this version does not know now reads "This app isn't available" instead of a blank page.

An App's Environment variables section now suggests the variable names its repository expects but that are not set yet, read from files such as `.env.example` and `vite-env.d.ts`, each with an Add button that fills in the name.

WhatsApp settings now end setup with a Try it step: a QR code, a link to open the chat and a few prompts to send. The same card opens from a number's menu. Link my phone shows a QR code and a tap-to-open link with the code, and it closes once the phone is linked. Try it is not offered for a paused number or one being released.
Saving a usage card inside the CodePress mobile app now opens the phone's share sheet with the image, on app builds that can save files.
Managed Apps opened on an App page record content-free Interactions into the organization's Apps project when this machine's telemetry setting is on.
An App collection's Interactions App now opens on its own page: the App UI Fixer switch and runs, the findings of the App it reports on, and a link to that App's screens.
The unified shell's Agent rail has an "On this Mac" tab right after Projects that lists the automations running on this machine and the ones that just ended, with a running dot on the tab.

CI only: pull requests run just the Terminal script tests (`test:scripts`) a change can reach, and a descriptive `package.json` edit or an unused tooling file no longer runs every Terminal test. Nothing in the app changes.

Settings → Organization now has six entries: General, People (Members, Teams, Connections), Integrations (Integrations, Platform MCP), Branding & dashboard (Branding, Dashboard, Navigation, Quicklinks), Billing & usage (Billing, Usage, Capacity, App hosting) and Audit. Each combined page shows its tabs under the title; Billing and Capacity still open the web page inside Settings, under the same tabs. The organization's default model is set on General ("Agent defaults") and your own on Agents ("Your default model"); LLM Provider Keys links to both. On General, members now see the admin-only controls disabled with a note instead of a save that fails. Old links to the previous pages still open the right tab.

CI only: Terminal integration tests now record which server functions each test file runs, and pull requests log the files that coverage would select beside the full run. Nothing ships to the app; release builds are unchanged.

When you open your own synced project from another machine, artifacts that have a cloud copy now load from it, so a large video plays at once instead of showing the 25 MB notice. Download for those artifacts saves the cloud copy. Artifacts without a cloud copy still load from the machine that holds the project.

CI runners: a new Jobs tab lists every finished job in your repositories, with where it ran, whether it passed (and the step it failed at), how long it waited and how long it took. Filter by result, where it ran, workflow, branch or PR and time range; select a job to see its step timeline, and compare each job's runs on your machines against Blacksmith. A finished job in Queue opens in Jobs.
A CodePress-managed App's Settings now has an Environment variables panel: public values are built into the App and Redeploy now applies them; secrets are the workspace's shared Backend secrets.

Test tooling only, with no change to the app: Terminal's `isolate: false` Vitest guard now restores env, working directory and exit code through the shared `scripts/vitest-process-state.mjs`, and the network guard contract also runs in a vmForks worker.

CI runners: admins can ask a CI machine to refresh its golden VM image ("Refresh when allowed") from the Images tab, which lists each request with who asked, when and what came of it. The App also loads its first read when it is opened in a background window.

Settings → You has one page per topic: Agent accounts, Preferences, Agents & models, Orchestrator and Computers. Preferences gains Terminal (font, scrolling, bell, links, GitHub Actions, Ghostty, appearance), Keyboard (shortcuts) and Notifications tabs; Orchestrator gains its On this device display options and the Repositories editor (subscription pins, Add rule, instructions) under On this computer; Computers merges My computers and Team computers. This computer's Keybindings, Orchestrator and My computers tabs, and Agents → Repositories, are gone, and links to them open their new place. Signed out, or without Orchestrator access, those controls stay where they were.

Settings → This computer has six tabs: General, Agents, Editor, Network & remote access, Storage and Activity. Voice is a section of General. Agent MCPs is Agents → MCPs, beside Behavior and Detection. File Viewer is named Editor and keeps its machine rows apart from its display rows. Local usage and GitHub Stats are Activity's two tabs. General's rarely changed switches (terminal compatibility, background management, Per-Tab History, Stop Leftover Processes on Tab Close and Reload Unresponsive Windows Quietly) sit in an Advanced fold, which opens by itself when one of them is not at its default. Every switch still saves and works as before, and links to the old tabs open their new place.

Artifacts that have a cloud copy now have a Link button beside Download. It copies a link that teammates open after signing in. The artifact's owner can also switch the link to Public, so anyone with it can open the file, or revoke it. A project or chat that isn't synced shows Link disabled with "Turn on sync to share a link". An Orchestrator now gets the link back from `publish_artifact` once the file has uploaded. It can also ask for it with the new `artifact_share_link` tool, and makes a link public only when you ask.
Onboarding's two-column frame is now a shared component the app can use; the app does not show it yet.

Personal settings now follow you to every computer you sign in on. That covers the editor's font, options and themes, the terminal theme you chose, Start with Agent, the sidebar filter and floating dashboard, whether you want desktop and completion notifications, your custom agent patterns, and the Orchestrator's 24-hour clock and build panel. You change them under You → Preferences → Terminal and You → Orchestrator. Imported themes, the agent command, linters and the OS notification permission stay on each computer. On a shared computer, each person keeps their own values.
Terminal's isolated Vitest projects run on the vmForks pool, so CI spends less CPU starting a process for every test file.

People served web onboarding v2 now see the app's onboarding in the same two-column frame as the web after they sign in: a step rail with the workspace and "Step N of M", a large title and the web's footer buttons. First run, Add workspace and Replay onboarding all use it; Welcome, Sign in and everyone else's onboarding are unchanged.

The thread composer's model menu offers Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro under Workers on a project on this machine, as Project settings and the kickoff already do, and the Gemini rows in every model menu drop their extra description line.

A synced copy's open Agent card reads its worker only when the worker moved, at most once every 15 seconds, and a rate-limit refusal shows a quiet "Updated … · refreshing again shortly" line instead of the red banner.

Set how much memory and how many cores automations may use on this machine, and how many run at once, in Settings under "Run my automations on this machine" or through `update_terminal_agent_settings`. Terminal reports the limits on its heartbeat and refuses a job past the run limit itself.

A synced copy now offers Gemini for the Orchestrator and the workers when its home machine's Antigravity CLI (`agy`) can run it. The home sends its own Gemini status with the settings, and the copy's model menu and Project settings name the home machine, including when it must sign in there.

Add "Take no new automations" to the "On this Mac" tab and Settings → This computer: the machine stops taking new automation runs while what already runs there finishes, and new runs go to your other machines or the cloud.
Keep active Desktop sessions streaming while the host window is hidden or its renderer stalls, using bounded native capture liveness, and let viewers retry host connection drops.
